A new method for generating three-dimensional discrete fracture matrices is introduced, employing a novel approach to mesh generation. The technique produces meshes that perfectly fit around fractures, which are modeled as one-dimensional surfaces. A computational framework, based on the Mimetic Finite Difference method, is developed to simulate fluid and heat flow through these meshes. To validate the approach, numerical experiments are conducted to compare traditional mesh generation techniques with the new method. These experiments examine the impact of different mesh generation strategies on the accuracy of simulations, particularly in cases where fractures interact with boundaries or each other. A numerical example demonstrates how the novel mesh generation approach leads to more accurate solutions, particularly regarding fracture volume and transport properties. Furthermore, a series of numerical experiments are conducted to assess the performance of the discrete fracture matrix framework, comparing different methods and verifying numerical results against known analytical solutions. These verifications confirm the accuracy of the present approach. The associated computational difficulties are also highlighted, including the creation of meshes with complex fractures, which require specialized algorithms. To address this challenge, a specific algorithm is developed to efficiently generate high-quality meshes with intricate fractures, reducing computational costs. The efficiency of this mesh generation method is then evaluated, with significant performance gains achieved. Overall, this research contributes to the development of an efficient and accurate numerical framework for flow and transport simulations through discrete fracture matrices, using a novel mesh generation approach that perfects the fracture representation. This may lead to newly-discovered numerical methods and insights, which could be valuable for numerical engineers and scientists working on similar projects. Additionally, this work lays the foundation for future research into multi-phase and multi-component simulations through these discrete fracture matrices, potentially enabling novel contributions in this area. This study introduces an original algorithm that enables a cohort of unmanned aerial vehicles to autonomously navigate through complex environments by using surface scanning. The algorithm leverages a registration technique commonly employed in computer vision to maintain formation and prevent collisions, relying only on local information and not external sensors. Real-world experiments were conducted to validate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm. Results from these experiments demonstrate that the proposed method allows the drones to retain a stable spatial organization and avoid obstacles, even in situations with limited visibility. The implementation of this algorithm using deep learning-based software was also a key focus of this research. A video showcasing the algorithm in action is available at https://youtu.be/7R3uWeFF_nk.

This research focuses on solving an optimal control issue for a system consisting of a large collection of interconnected state equations, which are individually represented by continuous-time Markov processes. These state equations are subject to a common control mechanism and a specific perturbation mechanism, resulting in a complex dynamic system. Given the high dimensionality of this system, we apply the mean-field approach to develop an analytical solution, which involves replacing the system's interactions with average statistical properties. This substitution enables us to model the system using a continuous-time stochastic differential equation, for which we have developed a novel solution method. This approach allows us to derive an optimal control solution both for stochastic differential equations and within the context of stochastic differential games. Our research further generalizes its findings to systems affected by fractional Brownian motion, utilizing the knowledge that fractional properties of this motion leads to distinct irregularities in the system's dynamics. Our analytical solutions, which include both a regular and irregular case, demonstrate the applications of mean-field approaches in developing novel analytical methods that utilize average statistical properties to solve complex high-dimensional dynamic systems. Ultimately, we also investigate the existence and uniqueness of the solution through an study on the different types of mean-field stochastic differential equations. This research is an extension of our previous work on mean-field stochastic differential equations, for which we have established the existence and uniqueness of the solution under specific conditions. This paper is a significant contribution to the field of optimal control, particularly in applications involving mean-field models that utilize fractional data, such as population dynamics analysis. We examine the energy spectrum of a Dirac operator with a periodic potential and demonstrate that its finite-band energies exhibit absolute continuity. Additionally, we establish the existence of elliptic finite-band energies within any bounded interval of the real number line. However, we find that infinite-band energies are always singular and that elliptic finite-band and infinite-band energies cannot coexist. This result is consistent with earlier findings by Kottos, Lenard, and Smilansky for the case of a non-periodic Dirac operator. Moreover, we identify the conditions under which quasi-Elliptic finite-band energies of a non-self-adjoint Dirac operator correspond to bounded solutions of a related classical elliptic equation. This connection reveals a link between the spectral theory of a Dirac operator and the solution space of a linear elliptic partial differential equation. Finally, we illustrate our findings via an example involving a periodic mass-spring system and demonstrate the computational efficacy of combining analytical and numerical techniques to study this problem. This approach enables the resolution of systems involving many degrees of freedom and low-frequency modes. Due to the vast degree of freedom in choosing the periodic potential, we anticipate that our method of combining analytical and numerical techniques will yield significant computational benefits in studying the spectral theory of a Dirac operator. RSUs are a vital component in V2X, facilitating communication with users; however, congestion areas are often poorly served due to high data traffic, weak signals, and interference, which can be addressed through the use of vehicle relays. To enhance the network in these situations, this research utilizes stochastic geometry to develop an innovative model for two-tier vehicular networks, incorporating the relaying function. The focus is on analyzing the success rate of relayed transmissions in vehicle networks and comparing the performance of different systems, including vehicle relay networks, conventional RSU-based networks, and general relay networks. The findings of this study indicate that vehicle relay networks perform better than conventional RSU-based networks, with an improved success rate; further, vehicle relay networks offer reduced success rate to that of general relay networks, with this advantage accompanied by the decrease in relay effectiveness. The results of this study suggest that RSUs, vehicle relays, and heterogeneous vehicular networks with vehicle relays could significantly increase the network success rate and are an essential part of these systems. The generalization of this study to cover more complex scenarios, such as vehicles with multi-antennas, and vehicle-assisted relays have also been examined in this research, which further highlights the potential of these systems to enhance network performance. The examination of this study reveals that in scenarios involving vehicles with multi-antennas, the success rate is affected by the number of antennas, with this success rate being highest when two antennas are used; the loss due to system processing, vehicle movement, and multi-antenna use is then compared to that of vehicle relay networks, with the latter performing better; finally, the success rates of RSU-based networks and vehicle-assisted relay networks were examined, with the latter performing better. The findings of this study suggest that vehicle relay networks are the most suitable for applications that require high data rates, such as telemetry traffic, while RSU-based networks are the most suitable for applications such as traffic control. The use of vehicle relays is recommended for telemetry traffic, with vehicle-assisted relay networks being the most suitable for applications such as video streaming. The code for this study has been shared on a public platform to facilitate further research and development. The contribution of this study can be broken down into developing an innovative model for two-tier vehicular networks, analyzing the success rate of relayed transmissions, comparing the performance of different systems, and investigating the performance of vehicle-assisted relay networks, which will enable future research to be conducted quickly and efficiently. Wikipedia's extensive collections of text can serve as a valuable resource for academic and commercial purposes, yet its content is often marred by inaccuracies and biases. Existing research focuses primarily on evaluating the quality of Wikipedia's content, with little consideration for its contributors and editing processes. By examining the behavioral patterns of Wikipedia editors, we aim to develop an unsupervised method for identifying and labeling problematic sections within articles. Through an in-depth analysis of editor actions and editor characteristics, we have pinpointed specific behaviors that indicate low quality content and developed a novel aggregation method to identify article sections requiring improvement. When tested on a predefined set of sensitive topics, our proposed approach outperformed existing quality assessment standards in accuracy and efficiency. Notably, our method exhibited exceptional results on smaller articles and collections lacking comprehensive quality assessments. While our research highlights the utility of investigating Wikipedia editors' behaviors, we also emphasize the potential dangers of automating quality assessment and urge further study of the implicit knowledge and biases embedded within editors' behavioral patterns. Ultimately, we contend that exploring Wikipedia editors' behaviors holds significant potential for discovering new patterns and insights that can improve the accuracy and relevance of Wikipedia's content. This study explores the concept of knowledge transfer in machine learning, focusing on transferring information from a robust machine learning model that makes decisions based on its internal structure. Typically, this involves moving knowledge from a detailed, complex model to a simpler model, with the goal of imposing the original model's decision-making rules on a less complex architecture. We investigate this challenge in a situation where the internal mechanics of the original model are unknown and cannot be accessed. Our approach to this problem relies on developing a novel black-box knowledge transfer technique that relies on a trustworthiness assessment of the original model and does not require knowledge of its internal workings. This transfer technique does not need any training parameters and can function effectively even with limited data. The accuracy of the transferred model is comparable to that of a model that has been trained from scratch on a large dataset. Notably, our proposed method does not involve any significant changes to the original model and can be utilized for different types of knowledge transfer without any adjustments. The efficacy of our approach is demonstrated through experiments involving simplified models of self-regulating cell membranes called chemostats and a biochemically realistic model of gene expression. These experiments confirm that under certain conditions, the knowledge transfer method can deliver results of the same quality as models that have complete knowledge of the system dynamics. The study also examines the relationship between knowledge quality and its transfer and analyzes the impact of noise on the transfer process. The findings highlight the potential of our proposed method to facilitate knowledge transfer in complex systems with limited information availability. The study's findings are further supported by the discovery of common patterns in the decision-making processes of different models. These patterns, known as approximations, offer insights into the internal workings of machine learning models and could have significant implications for fields such as neuroscience and artificial intelligence. The study provides a range of tools, including a method for detecting approximations in decision-making processes, and explores their potential for modeling learning as a process of approximating these patterns. The research demonstrates that approximations can be learned through a process of reverse knowledge transfer. The study also employs approximations to examine the relationship between the internal workings of machine learning models and their behavior. The study further utilizes approximations to develop a novel transfer technique that exploits similarities in the decision-making processes of different models. The non-regularity of the projection map's twisted differential and the presence of a twisted connection beta are key aspects that allow us to apply T-duality. This paper tackles the code-distance metric and decoding methods for PAC codes. Unlike previous approaches, we directly calculate PAC codes using a simplified metric that circumvents the usual union bound, thereby yielding tighter error bounds. Our approach also enables simplified decoding schemes, particularly one that achieves optimal performance on infinite-dimensional spaces, without requiring further approximation. This allows us to accurately calculate PAC code rates. The advantages of our method are demonstrated through specific examples. Additionally, we successfully developed a computational tool to calculate PAC code rates, making it easily accessible via an online interface. Furthermore, our work extends PAC code principles to cover cases involving continuous variables, paving the way for novel applications in physics-based coding tasks. Specifically, we successfully developed a protocol for transmitting classical and quantum messages across lossy quantum channels and established a fundamental limit on achievable rates for such channels. The computed protocols achieve optimal performance in several scenarios, including when the channel gain is unknown or follows a specific distribution. The developed tool can be accessed at: https://paco-qin.github.io/PACCodeTool/. This research was funded through various funding sources, including NSF, NLR, and DARPA. We introduce a novel hand-tracking approach called HandTracker3D, which synchronizes point cloud sequences captured by sensors in everyday environments. HandTracker3D accurately interprets the movements and transformations of individual hands, enabling its operation in two modes: a straightforward, general hand-tracking mode and a more complex mode that identifies and links three-dimensional items grabbed by hands. HandTracker3D's stability and precision are demonstrated through evaluations on public datasets and a newly created, challenging sequence dataset crafted from public video datasets by converting them into 3D point cloud format. HandTracker3D consistently outperforms other state-of-the-art methods in terms of both accuracy and computational efficiency, making it suitable for real-world, embedded systems such as robots and wearable devices. HandTracker3D's code and the created dataset are openly accessible for further research and development. Experimental analysis into the newly created dataset reveals the intricacies of human-hand interactions and items grabbed by hands, which can be utilized by the hand tracking community to address open research questions and improve state-of-the-art hand tracking approaches. Furthermore, HandTracker3D enables numerous applications in human-robot interaction such as identifying and reconstructing the tasks being performed, the items handed over, and the final state of the environment following a interaction event. These capabilities are freely accessible and can be easily integrated into ground robots and wearable devices for enhanced functionality. Embedding HandTracker3D on an Amazon Deep Learning camera allowed us to demonstrate its efficacy in real-time hand tracking and reconstruction of grabbed items within everyday scenes. This real-time capability further validates HandTracker3D's efficiency and accuracy under dynamic, ambient conditions. Nonetheless, the hand tracking community still remains unresolved and further work is needed to achieve reliable and error-free hand tracking in diverse and dynamic environments. In particular, item reconstruction and tracking of specific items grabbed by hands in diverse environments remain open problems and require further research to achieve reliable results, especially when viewing hand poses. Additionally, when viewing hand poses, it remains uncertain which hand is utilizing which, even after analyzing numerous hand poses, and identifying these hand-to-item correlations remains uncertain and requires further research to achieve reliable results. This paper has now initiated this area of research and provided a hand tracking approach called HandTracker3D that accurately interprets the movements and interactions of individual hands in diverse environments, but also leaves these problems unresolved and provides a new dataset for further investigation. This dataset, called HandItem, is comprised of over a thousand thousand frames captured from multiple viewpoints, where the interaction between hands and items is manually reconstructed and annotated

A novel, training-based method is developed to determine the optimal position and orientation of a robot's end-effector in real-time, utilizing data from a depth camera without relying on specific markers. A deep neural network is created by combining image data with corresponding robot action information, enabling the model to make precise predictions. Performance is evaluated across various scenarios, with results showing the model can accurately localize its end-effector across diverse environments and conditions. Furthermore, by incorporating the estimated pose, the model can accurately track the movement of objects and robots, outperforming traditional optical-based localization methods. With its reliable pose estimation, the model can facilitate a range of applications, including augmented reality, where the proposed method is initially validated. A comprehensive video supplement is available online to showcase the model's performance and training. 

Keywords: Augmented Reality, Deep Learning, End-Effector Pose Estimation, Robot Localization, Markerless tracking.

Therapy interference occurs when one patient's treatment benefits decline due to another patient's treatment.  This phenomenon has significant implications for healthcare providers and regulators, who must assess a drug's safety and efficacy before allowing it to enter the market.  Currently, there is a lack of standard methods for detecting therapy interference; as a result, some important conclusions have been drawn incorrectly in past studies.  This research develops a novel approach for identifying therapy interference using a model called the K-neighborhood interference model, which assumes that a patient interacts with every other patient within a certain number of patients.  This study presents an efficient algorithm for estimating the parameters of the K-neighborhood interference model and testing the superiority of one treatment over another through statistical analysis.  The proposed method is challenging because model estimation is difficult: the number of possible parameter settings is vast, and it is difficult to model patient interactions as independent events.  To address these issues, the proposed method uses a simulation-based approach to narrow down the range of possible parameter settings and performs a parametric test on the remaining options.  This method is challenging because when we restrict the range of possible parameter settings, the test's statistical validity is no longer certain.  This study presents an innovative simulation-based approach to address this problem and provides a comprehensive framework for testing the superiority of one treatment over another under the K-neighborhood interference model.  The proposed methods are validated through numerical simulations and real-world data analysis on a specific anti-inflammatory drug's safety and efficacy.  The results show that the proposed methods detect significant declines in treatment benefits when one patient's treatment benefits decline due to another patient's treatment and suggest strategies for improving the drug's future treatment.  This study presents two important contributions to the field of clinical trial inference.  First, it develops a novel approach for estimating the parameters of the K-neighborhood interference model and testing the superiority of one treatment over another through statistical analysis, addressing a long-standing gap in current research.  Second, this study provides comprehensive evidence of therapy interference in a real-world drug, highlighting the significance of detecting such interference in assessing a drug's safety and efficacy. However, by assuming a two-body annihilation process and a specific medium-dependent interaction mechanism, approximate expressions for neutrino emissions can be derived. Our research introduces ShapePipe, an innovative pipeline designed for accurate galaxy shape measurement that outperforms other leading pipelines, including SHARP, MetaCAIRN, and DILATED. In our study, ShapePipe's performance was assessed on the CFIS data, yielding an 88% agreement rate with S20 data in terms of shape measurement. The pipeline's 83rd percentile computation time was a mere 45 seconds per arcminute. Furthermore, our analysis reveals a 5% decrease in bias compared to MetaCAIRN and a 10% decrease compared to DILATED. To facilitate public access, our research includes detailed documentation and publicly accessible datasets, including 750,000 Jy09 galaxies with shape information. Our findings demonstrate that ShapePipe's influence is 0.03 and 0.06 for 4500deg and 9000deg, respectively, with an intrinsic dispersion of 0.15. Our research also covers the accurate reconstruction of mass maps as well as the mitigation of systematic biases through the application of mean-field modeling. The mean-field model has successfully eliminated the systematic bias, with our map's 0-order and 1-order RMS values amounting to 250 and 620 arcseconds, respectively. Our research data, including detailed documentation and publicly accessible datasets, can be accessed at the following URL: https://github.com/ShapePipe/ShapePipe-Repository/tree/main/S1_5.0.1_release.olt.ROI_packed.h5. The growing demand for SRAM-based architectures in machine learning, automation testing, and random number generation has led to increased requirements for their reliability. Since SRAM cells can produce randomness as a by-product, their utilization in these fields has been limited by the need to access and exploit this randomness. A novel technique, TuRaN, utilizes a method to extract and utilize the inherent randomness of SRAM cells without needing to access them directly through a and B. TuRaN achieves this by reducing the operating voltage and utilizing a feedback loop to select the desired output, allowing for the production of random bits at high speeds while only consuming one SRAM cell at the expense of energy consumption. TuRaN's performance was evaluated in a 28nm process node and demonstrated to produce over 1GC/s of random bits with an energy efficiency of 100fJ/bit at 225MHz while staying within a 5x undervoltage boundary. Additionally, TuRaN was tested to determine its resistance to data corruption and random number generation failures, revealing a specific correlation between these phenomena and the level of voltage undervolting. TuRaN's performance was then compared to other methods, showing its superiority particularly at low voltage levels. Overall, TuRaN's capabilities make it an attractive solution for applications at the edge of energy-efficient, high-speed random number generation capabilities. TuRaN's code is publicly available on GitHub under the link https://github.com/espinoul/TuRaN. TuRaN's simulation environment, including the 28nm process model, can be accessed through sopcinfo at https://sopcinfo.eecs.ualberta.ca/. TuRaN's compiler has been integrated into this platform and is also separately available as open-source software under the MIT License. TuRaN's hardware components can be fabricated through the SkyW water2sim tool at https://skyw.eecs.ualberta.ca/. TuRaN's designers, including the compiler, can also be designed using this platform. TuRaN's noise properties were evaluated using SkyW's capability to simulate 28nm process node characteristics. TuRaN's resilience was then tested using SkyW's verification tool to determine data corruption and number generation failures in different undervolting conditions. TuRaN was finally compared to other designs through SkyW's design space exploration feature that identified its optimal parameters for reliable and efficient random number generation. Furthermore, certain properties of the Reynolds number can be trivially violated in low-dimensional quantum fluids due to zero-dimensional semi conductors. We examine the unique properties of the Reynolds number in quantum Hall fluids and their equivalents, focusing on the thermal Hall systems. Finally, we consider the effect of an arbitrary potential on the Reynolds number's distribution functions and find that certain properties can be generalized to specific systems while maintaining their physical significance. The findings of this study may contribute to further research in quantum thermal pumps and hydrodynamics, enabling the exploration of new phenomena and insights. Marginal dependence models, which we'll refer to as MDMs, represent a type of model used to capture relationships between continuous variables, assuming that their interdependence can be understood through a functional relationship in their distributions' parameters. These models have various applications, particularly in studying non-linear connections, and a comprehensive overview of them has been absent in existing literature. This work aims to classify MDMs, according to their functional forms, and examine their distinct characteristics in order to determine their combined efficacy for future research purposes. Several data-driven approaches are introduced for selecting the most suitable MD dimensions, and the benefits and limitations of naive moment-based estimators for identifying dependencies are explored. The performance of naive estimators is further evaluated through simulations under various scenarios, and a case study analyzing the relationship between HDI health indicators and life expectancy outcomes is conducted, utilizing both a data-driven and a selection method based on principal components. The findings show that naive estimators can provide reliable insights into dependent structures, particularly in contexts where the underlying relationships are not linear. The analysis also reveals that the most variable components often hold the key to understanding distributions' dependencies, and future research directions in this field are proposed. This study investigates how the US earnings distribution evolves over different life stages and what impact age has on the distribution's shape. We develop a theoretical model to explain this observation. In this model, every stage of life offers its own set of career opportunities, which are distributed unevenly among the population, resulting in variations in life-long earnings. Our simulation shows that the opportunities can be seen as a representation of the chances for success, which are essential for fair social mobility policies. These policies often concentrate on supporting disadvantaged youth; however, our research indicates that the opportunities affecting inequality can arise from various sources of disruption, such as family background or socio-economic status, which may not always be associated with youth. We propose several potential interventions aimed at reducing the influence of opportunity disruption and, subsequently, income inequality among the youth demographic. These ideas may inform discussions around social mobility with young individuals and their families. Ultimately, our study offers a new perspective on the concept of opportunities and how they contribute to the complex issue of income inequality. We introduce a new measure called space toughness to analyze the stability of solving linear systems, particularly in the context of iterative methods and preconditioning. This measure assesses how much a given solver's solution quality deteriorates when subjected to arbitrary perturbations in the system's matrix and right-hand side. Since it accounts for perturbations in both the matrix and right-hand side, it offers a more comprehensive understanding than simply considering a loss of convergence or condition number amplification. We demonstrate that space toughness is a coherent and strong indicator of solution quality deterioration and provide a series of solvers arranged in ascending order of toughness. We then conduct numerical experiments to verify that solvers with higher space toughness are more resilient to arbitrary matrix and right-hand side perturbations. Moreover, we observe that solvers with higher space toughness also exhibit greater tolerance for ill-conditioned matrices, particularly in cases where the eigenvalue spectrum is centered around zero. Building upon this concept, we also define time toughness to evaluate solver behavior over multiple iterations and provide numerical verification of time toughness's accuracy. Our research further includes the open-source implementation of over 50 solvers in Python and C++ that can be accessed through an easy-to-use interface, enabling reproducible results and facilitating additional solver additions. A wide range of additional solers can be easily integrated due to the provided code. Traditional machine learning methods may generate models that are suitable for predictive purposes but lack the guaranteed safety requirements. This work presents a groundbreaking approach that leverages learning from other stakeholders to establish a safe and reliable model. We employ a non-convex optimization method with robust regularization to develop a unique representation of the system's dynamics and develop an efficient gradient descent procedure for effective parameter selection. To ensure the model's safety, we utilize techniques such as formula-based and reachability analysis to assess potential system outcomes. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in modeling a power grid system involving multiple stakeholders, each with distinct knowledge of the system. These stakeholders can provide data in the form of time-series patterns or frequency and duration combinations. Experimental results show that our model, which incorporates data from all stakeholders, outperforms other methods by accurately identifying system patterns and minimizing potential safety risks. Galaxy cluster observations have primarily focused on the formation of cooling cores, yet little is known about the initial stages of cluster cooling. This study employs one-dimensional simulations to examine the dynamics of gas clouds sinking into the potential well of a galaxy cluster, similar to those seen in simulations of galaxy merger interactions. The cloud's lower cloud edge is fixed at a specified radius, causing it to accumulate mass and energy as it collapses under gravity, leading to a non-equilibrium gas distribution and increased entropy within the core. We consider two types of clouds: radiative cooling clouds, enveloped by a steep density gradient, and non-cooling clouds subject to thermal conduction. The latter's heat balance is influenced by a balance between thermal conduction and work done by turbulent motions. We introduce a parameter for effective thermal conductivity that adjusts based on the power of turbulent motions that is dissipated within the cloud. This parameter allows our model to self-consistently reproduce the observed broadening of X-ray spectra in the feedback radius of galaxy clusters. Furthermore, our results show that non-cooling clouds may eventually lead to the development of a cooling core, primarily through mechanical means, whereas radiative cooling clouds do not require an additional source of energy to initiate a core formation. We also explore how magnetic fields affect our model, specifically by increasing the effective thermal conductivity due to increased diffusion and collision rates. Ultimately, our results provide a framework for understanding the formation and evolution of cooling cores and related feedback processes in galaxy clusters. They also offer a way to model gas clouds using fewer free parameters, specifically the effective thermal conductivity that is in good agreement with recent observations. This approach could be applied to numerical simulations of galaxy cluster formation to provide further physical insights. From an observational perspective, our model suggests that the power spectra of IR emission from galaxy clusters could be influenced by both cooling and non-cooling processes, whereas X-ray spectra within certain energy ranges may be influenced by thermal conduction and turbulent motions. Furthermore, our model predicts that the effective thermal conductivity should vary depending on the mass of galaxy clusters. This property could be verified through future observations using Chandra and XMM-Newton satellites for hotter clusters. Finally, our results imply that galaxy clusters may experience periodic 'heat bursts,' characterized by a sharp increase in X-ray brightness, primarily due to the cloud's collapse and subsequent internal energy release. This phenomenon may be detected in the near future through sensitive observations of X-ray spectra using large galaxy clusters. This research explores the feasibility of creating a voice without prior knowledge of the speaking individual, language, or phonetic rules, based solely on acoustic models of sentence-level units. To circumvent the need for transcription, we utilize a wide range of sentences from a single language, breaking them down into fixed-length units and developing a neural network that learns to represent these units both auditorially and vocally. A similar unit-based approach is applied to transcription, and we develop a neural network that learns to generate audio from these transcribed units. However, since we lack direct access to the units, we utilize a wide range of sentences to learn a universal unit encoder. A neural network that learns to approximate the visual transcription of these units is also developed. While this method does not utilize written transcriptions, it does rely on a large amount of data and a large number of speakers to learn a universal set of units. We successfully demonstrated that this method is possible to the level of human-like clarity, although our tests were limited to a single individual speaking a single language.

We investigated the movement patterns of a cup filled with coffee being placed on a vibrating surface to replicate the conditions of a forced pendulum. The average period of oscillation was measured for varying angles of inclination and vibrational frequencies. The results demonstrated that the average period increased with greater inclinations and achieved a maximum value at an average rate of 5.06 times that of its unmoved state. Furthermore, we observed an average length change of 2.08 for the largest studied inclination of 84 degrees. Using our experimental findings, we verified how oscillation patterns are affected by factors including effective length and force. The relationship between these variables was found to be nonlinear, especially at more pronounced inclinations. Additionally, we recorded and analyzed videos of the oscillations, which revealed average amplitude reductions of 0.53 to 3.09 compared to the unmoved state. The amount of reduction increased with more pronounced inclinations. Based on our results, we suggest a new formula to estimate oscillation periods that is 1.03 times greater than the classical approximation and accurate to at least 10% of the unmoved state for a wide range of conditions. We demonstrate that the net effect of solar radiation pressure's differential force is to increase an orbit's semi-major axis, with the magnitude of this change maximized at 0.06 AU over a 10-year period. We also establish through numerical modeling that a significant portion, approximately 50%, of all low Earth orbits will experience a semi-secular resonance impact within a 10-year frame. It is noteworthy that while the resonance's influence on perigee height exhibits variability, it generally results in heightened variability under conditions of increased eccentricity. Moreover, we identify that approximately half of all low Earth orbits with eccentricities greater than 0.6 will be affected by the resonance within a 10-year window. Tight-binding models, which describe atomic orbitals with Gaussian functions, are commonly used to approximate the behavior of electrons in solid materials and molecules. Although these models are simple and easy to work with, they have a major drawback: the lack of unitarity in the approximation, which affects the accuracy of certain calculations. In relation to this issue, we investigate how the unitarity of light-matter interactions is preserved in tight-binding models, specifically through the use of first-principle and semi-classical models that account for electron spin and position. Our analysis reveals that only certain distributions of atomic orbitals can ensure perfect light-matter unitarity, and we demonstrate this through a variational approach in one dimension. In order to maintain unitarity, we propose modifying electron states by introducing 'dipole friction', which effectively adjusts the position of electrons based on their momentum. This fricition is shown to be responsible for a broad range of photon-matter interactions, and we verify its relevance through a range of examples, including basic and complex systems. Furthermore, we find that a range of equivalent methods can also preserve unitarity, such as using Gaussian functions with properly chosen variances or 'orbital squeezing' to control electron states. In conclusion, we identify the specific conditions required for unitarity in tight-binding models and provide a range of methods to achieve this goal. These findings offer insights into the fundamental nature of electron interactions and may influence the design of future electron-based devices. Additionally, our analysis reveals that perfect unitarity in tight-binding models is tied to a particular property of light, which we call 'dipolar purity'. In other words, the distribution of electronic states approximating electron position must be 'dipolar' in nature - meaning that the second central moment of the distribution is zero - for the approximation to be unitary. Interestingly, this 'dipolar purity' criterion can be thought of as an analogue of a fundamental property of light known as'monopolar purity'. While perfect unitarity may be impossible in certain scenarios, our analysis reveals that approximations with very low errors can be achieved under specific conditions. These findings are expected to influence theoretical research in related fields such as solid-state physics and chemistry, as well as in quantum optics and information science, particularly in regards to the development of future devices that rely on electron-based light-matter interactions. This study investigates the properties of a confidence interval for the mean of a Cauchy distribution, demonstrating that the conventional approach yields drastically wider intervals than necessary when the parameters $\mu$ and $\sigma$ are unknown. Ultimately, this research establishes that specifying a minimum coverage probability of $1-C$ necessitates assigning a minimum sample size of $n > (1/C)\ln(2/\alpha)$. A corresponding lower bound is determined for the width of these confidence intervals, with further analysis conducted to optimize this width in the case of paired data. A similar investigation is then performed for the standard deviation of a Cauchy distribution, with the same framework and findings applied. Lastly, this research examines the minimum required sample sizes for testing the means of two independent Cauchy distributions and uncorrelated Cauchy variables, with specific values calculated for commonly used confidence levels. Finally, simulations are employed to illustrate the theoretical results and examine the performance of the proposed methods. These proposals can also be extended to other distributions with heavy tails. \\

A new statistical approach assesses the sample size requirements for clinical trials where treatment effects are evaluated across different patient subgroups within a single trial design. This method considers factors like variance, success rates, and desired effect sizes to calculate the needed trial participants. To further optimize accuracy, we've developed a Bayesian technique that allows for information sharing between these subgroups. We compared the accuracy of this Bayesian approach with traditional methods in various clinical trial settings. Results show the Bayesian approach maintains statistical integrity in scenarios with similar success rates across subgroups, but may compromise results when there's significant difference in success rates between the subgroups of interest. We found our Bayesian approach has limitations in scenarios with limited knowledge of the subgroups' success rates, leading to inflated type II error rates. Despite these drawbacks, the Bayesian approach has potential advantages, and we suggest combining it with other methods like adaptive randomization to further optimize its performance. We present numerical results from various simulations conducted to evaluate these findings. To our knowledge, this study pioneers the assessment of basket trials' sample size requirements using a Bayesian approach that temporarily borrows information between subgroups. High-performance motion control systems have become indispensable for many advanced industrial applications. To meet the growing demands for system precision, parameter variability in these systems must be carefully considered in the design. Traditional linear control designs that assume fixed system parameters may not be sufficient. To address this, this study presents a parameterized control design method for high-precision motion control systems using a sequential loop tightening approach. The approach involves iterating through successive loops of system models, incorporating increasing levels of system uncertainty with each iteration, until a desired level of control performance is achieved. To evaluate the proposed control design, this study employs a flexible motion system with variable mass distribution, known as the flexible test bed for automated control experiments (FTBE). When compared to conventional linear control designs, the proposed LPV control design yields significantly improved performance, demonstrating a 50% improvement in setpoint tracking accuracy and a 30% improvement in robustness to system parameter variations. Furthermore, the study highlights the practical feasibility of the proposed control design by demonstrating its implementation on the FTBE using a Texas Instruments digital signal processor. Experimental results confirm the predicted performance outcomes of the proposed design. To further validate the proposed control design, the study includes comparison analyses with other advanced control designs, such as the minimal incremental rate approach and the multi-objective control approach, demonstrating its superior performance over these methods. In terms of computational complexity, the study reveals that the proposed control design requires a more computationally intensive approach than other advanced control designs but remains computationally feasible for real-time hardware implementation. Specifically, the study shows that the proposed control design requires a 76 ms sampling time on a Texas Instruments digital signal processor, which is significantly shorter than the 100 ms time limit specified by the test bed's hardware and software developers. In conclusion, the proposed LPV control design has demonstrated superior performance over other control designs while remaining computationally feasible for real-time hardware implementation. We introduce a general, flexible framework called Partial Registration Network (PRNet), designed specifically for aligning partial point cloud views. Building on learning-based methods, PRNet employs deep convolutional networks to overcome the limitations posed by partial visibility. Unlike existing methods which rely on complete or surface-based views, PRNet leverages partially overlapping sections both for self-supervised learning and alignment. A key component of PRNet involves a flexible self-overlap module that enables double registration for robust alignment. Through extensive evaluation on challenging datasets such as SENSORSE, ObjectFX and AreaFest, we demonstrate PRNet's superior performance compared to state-of-the-art techniques across various benchmark tests. Furthermore, we showcase PRNet's real-world applicability in vehicle localization using sensor data. Thorough experimentation and analysis solidify PRNet's potential as a reliable choice for partial point cloud alignment. In medical image segmentation, the lack of fully annotated datasets and the reliance on region-based methods that use adjacent pixel information hinder more accurate tissue identification, particularly in MRI scans with its varying modalities and high resolution. Most existing methods treat different modalities as separate images and ignore their interdependencies, while some attempts incorporate multi-modality information but through labor-intensive data alignment. This paper addresses these challenges by designing a method that simultaneously segmentates multiple modalities, integrates information across them, and achieves cyclic division of individual modality images. Through extensive evaluation on two public datasets, the proposed approach demonstrates superior performance compared to current state-of-the-art techniques. For example, it achieves an Dice-Sorensen score of 78.8% on the MSOAR-RS dataset for ADC+T2WI tissue classification. The associated code and datasets can be found at https://github.com/Saivion/CyclicDivGAN. Experimental findings also highlight the method's sensitivity to parameter settings and dataset size, paving the way for further research in fully unsupervised segmentation using synthetic data. Finally, the developed approach facilitates fully automated tissue segmentation from MRI scans without the need for fully annotated labels, enabling faster and more efficient clinical processes. The proposed method may contribute to cost reduction in clinical settings by quickly providing rough tissue segmentation as an initial step, although further study is needed on using these rough labels as input for fully supervised techniques to approach human-level accuracy. Overall, the proposed approach successfully addresses the long-standing issue of limited annotation data and fully supervised training costs in medical image segmentation through unsupervised learning. Moreover, it shows promise in reducing clinical costs through semi-supervised learning using fully automated tissue segmentation as a starting point. To validate its potential in clinical settings, parameter optimization was performed based on dataset size, yielding the best results for specific applications. Finally, the developed method may approach human-level accuracy when used in combination with fully supervised techniques that utilize its rough labels as input. To verify this potential, we performed semi-supervised learning using the fully automated tissue segmentation produced by the proposed approach as labels for fully supervised state-of-the-art techniques, resulting in improved performance when only a small number of labels are available. This strategy may contribute to reducing costs in clinical settings by quickly providing rough tissue segmentation, and we plan to continue investigating its application. This research presents a novel neural architecture, named Feature Mapping RNN (FM-RNN), whose core is a key component in generating features for action prediction. FM-RNN leverages a radial basis function (RBF) to transform its internal state into a higher-dimensional space, where feature mapping functions are learned through backpropagation. We integrate FM-RNN with a Markov decision process (MDP) model, dubbed Radial Basis Function MDP (RBMDF), which leverages the generated features. Our method's effectiveness is demonstrated through action prediction in three complex video datasets: JHMDB-21, UCF101-24, and Charades-24. Furthermore, the implications of the results for predicting other flare types were explored. A newly created hydrogen boride compound, existing in a monolayer form, exhibits potential as a key component in the creation of superconducting materials. Like other 2D superconductors, it has an unusual feature in that it's typically not stable off a specific substrate, however we found that it's more resilient than initially thought. Through the use of a layered van der Waals binding model, we identified that the monolayer hydrogen boride's stability is primarily influenced by its chemical bond, with the addition of phosphorus improving its stability. While phosphorus does enhance the stability, it also hinders the superconducting properties, causing a complete loss at a certain concentration level, with the superconducting properties being partially restored at another level, with the superconducting transition temperature (Tc) reaching as high as 5.93 K. Overall, P-doped hydrogen boride (HPbxHby) has the potential for practical application due to its 2D stability and strong superconducting properties. To ensure the stability of the system, particularly when subjected to mechanical pressure, we found that it's essential for the number of phosphorus atoms to be an odd number. The incorporation of phosphorus results in significant differences in the material's electronic, vibrational, and superconducting properties. The electronic structure reveals an increased dose of electrons, with the formation of a new chemical bond, while the phonon spectrum shows that the lowest-frequency vibrational mode's frequency significantly decreases, primary responsible for the superconducting phenomenon in hydrogen boride, thus indicating that the superconductivity in this material is mediated by electrons interacting with this phonon. The ultimate impact of these changes on the material's Tc was also simulated and predicted. The 2D Tc values we calculated (5.93 K) are significantly higher than those in experiments (1.56 K), with the latter value being closest to the 3D limit (1.31 K), with our results indicating the potential for an even higher Tc in this system. The study has led to a greater understanding (and prediction) of how phosphorus affects the superconducting properties of hydrogen boride, with variations in the number of phosphorus atoms resulting in distinct physical changes, making P-doped hydrogen boride a promising material for superconductivity. The theoretical research has provided essential knowledge on how to develop and improve 2D superconductors. The research data can be accessed through the doi: 10.6084/m1.fm

The underlying architecture of High Performance Computing (HPC) systems relies on a multicore socket configuration. Still, the hardware and software interfaces make it difficult to optimize application performance due to hidden abstraction levels.  We propose a run allocation method over flattened partitions (RAMAP) that provides a direct mapping between logical threads and physical cores through a multi-level graph representation.  We compare the efficacy of RAMAP with the default Linux thread scheduling in an HPC environment across various workloads including compressive sensing, the Poisson-Boltzmann equation, and the simulation of sparse matrix and dense vector operations.  Our results show that RAMAP improves overall system scalability and outperforms default scheduling in most cases, particularly when applications exhibit balanced core allocation.  However, we also observed instances where default scheduling performed better, especially with asymmetric workload distributions on eight-core nodes.  Nevertheless, we believe that the proposed RAMAP approach presents a simple and efficient solution for optimizing thread scheduling in HPC systems.  Our code and associated results are accessible via GitHub for reproducibility purposes.  We hope that the proposed method will contribute to the ongoing research in HPC optimization and encourage the community to explore new approaches in this domain.  Further experiments and evaluations are needed to confirm the performance of RAMAP in a broader range of scenarios.  It is also recommended that the Linux community considers incorporating a scheduling method similar to RAMAP in future Linux releases to leverage the potential for performance improvements. This paper outlines the reasoning behind validating a fail-operational automotive driving system using formal methods. We utilize Case Studies to identify and analyze potential system failures and evaluate the effectiveness of safety mechanisms, ultimately ensuring that system integrity is maintained even in the event of a failure. An example of a fail-operational system is a vehicle with an advanced driver-assistance system, where sudden and abrupt actions are still permitted to prevent collisions, even if a critical system fails. Building on previous research, our work focuses on driving systems that can initiate rapid maneuvers to prevent impacts. To ensure system safety, we develop and implement a formal model that leverages Camille, a tool for modeling and verifying dynamic systems with a focus on safety properties. Camille's modeling language allows for the description of a driving system using state machines and relations, facilitating the analysis of system failures and their impact on safety requirements. Our approach to validating fail-operational systems involves verifying two key conditions: (1) rapid actions can only be triggered safely, and (2) these actions must consistently maintain system safety. Through successive model transformations, camille's verifiers help validate both conditions, ultimately ensuring that system failures and driver-intervention-induced states do not compromise safety requirements. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of formal methods in validating fail-operational systems by facilitating the verification of system failures and its impact on safety requirements. Our model can be accessed through http://camille.inria.fr/models. We intend to extend our research by further exploring how system failures and changes in environmental conditions, such as road conditions and weather, impact vehicle safety and perform validation of fail-functional automotive driving systems. This research is original and follows the guidelines outlined in the 2022 ACM-KEOD journal special issue on applying formal methods to advanced driver-assistance systems. This work is a revised and updated version of our original research presented at the 2022 Model Engineering for Safety and Security Conference. A new approach, impact-based clustering, is developed for grouping dynamic systems using their behavioral patterns. It utilizes a dynamic system's responses, tracked over various parameters, to assess similarity among systems and form clusters. Traditional clustering methods are primarily applied to static data sets, making existing techniques and efficient clustering algorithms ineffective for dynamic systems. To address this, a new data representation is proposed, leveraging the system's dynamics, and subsequently, existing algorithms can be utilized for impact-based clustering. The method's efficacy is demonstrated through numerical experiments where actual parameter values are used to define groups, and results are further analyzed under uncertainty in these parameters. Compared to current methods, impact-based clustering demonstrates superior performance in identifying genuine groups in dynamic systems. It becomes an essential tool for researchers studying dynamical systems who aim to analyze and organize their findings. In particular, this approach is highly relevant to planetary science where scientists strive to categorize various celestial bodies and their dynamics based on behaviorally relevant characteristics. Furthermore, this technique has the potential for application in numerous other fields such as machine learning and bioinformatics. This essay offers an examination of three distinct mathematical treatments for Leibnizian calculus. We draw on a wealth of historical information about Leibniz's views on calculus and use this knowledge to build models that accurately reflect his understanding of the subject. The models are evaluated against key Leibnizian ideas and their ability to capture his philosophical stance on calculus is evaluated. One model is based on variable tender, another on a differential framework, and the final model incorporates a hybrid approach drawing from smooth calculus and nonstandard analysis. We find that the differential model is particularly effective in representing Leibnizian calculus and discuss how it aligns with many of Leibnizian insights. Furthermore, this approach has a natural extension that addresses some of the challenges posed by the nature of infinitesimal calculus. The essay also explores potential applications and implications of this framework, particularly in relation to a broader philosophical and physical context. The discussion is centered on the following main arguments. Firstly, the infinitesimal calculus of Leibniz is inherently connected to a tender approach to variables, an idea that is historically grounded and provides a clear understanding of his views on calculus. This approach is seen as a key introduction to a more comprehensive methodology for dealing with mathematical and physical problems. The tender framework is seen as a fundamental concept in the development of a scientific language that is consistent with the computational demands of calculus. The second argument concerns the fundamental role of a nilpotent differential in capturing the essence of Leibnizian calculus. This view is supported by various historical observations and is seen as providing a clear understanding of many key Leibnizian ideas. The third argument is based on a combination of smooth and nonstandard analysis methods that offers a robust framework for a well-developed calculus that is consistent with the computational demands of a scientific language. This approach is seen as a compromise between the tender framework and the nonstandard approach, and provides a flexible method for dealing with a wide range of mathematical and physical problems. We note, however, that although the nonstandard approach is seen as an extension of the hybrid model, it is not clear if it is possible to maintain a distinction between a computational language and an inferential language as described in this essay. Finally, we discuss the relevance and potential applications of this framework, particularly in relation to a broader philosophical and physical context. We examine the relationship between this approach and other metaphysical and epistemological aspects of calculus, and explore the implications of this relationship for our understanding of these issues. We provide a comprehensive outline for a proof that stands at the intersection of Ramsey theory and functional analysis, demonstrating that any operation across a wide range of Banach spaces still preserves Ramsey properties, even when applied across an infinite number of dimensions. This proof utilizes a previously established concept in an essentially equivalent form, inferring key insights from a more fundamental theorem within Ramsey theory. Alongside this, we explore the background of Ramsey theory, taking a comprehensive approach to cover the essential results leading up to a fundamental theorem known as the infinite Ramsey theorem, particularly focusing on the contributions and findings of mathematicians Komlós, Kalai, and Matu\v{s}elovi\'c. Furthermore, we analyze the extent to which the infinite Ramsey theorem's characteristics can be applied to the context of infinite-extent independent sets within the realm of Banach spaces, establishing a theoretical framework that may be utilized to formulate conjectures related to the partition calculus of infinite-extent Ramsey theory. Finally, we explore the partition complexity of partial functions, defining the concept and establishing a simplified yet robust version of a result initially proven by Matu\v{s}elovi\'c. This outcome holds potential for further development, potentially enabling the determination of the cardinality upper limit for the additivity number $\mathrm{Add}(\kappa)$ within the partition calculus of infinite-extent Ramsey theory. However, this limit remains unknown for $\kappa\geq\aleph_2$ and remains open for further investigation. We propose a new direction for this research, specifically exploring the partition complexity of functions with at most two values, while also outlining further possible avenues for research in this area. Additionally, we collected and compiled a list of open problems and conjectures within Ramsey theory and infinite-extent partition calculus, particularly focusing on a fundamental question in Ramsey theory that has remained unsolved for decades: determining whether it is possible to partition a set $\mathcal{P}$ of infinite-dimensional Banach spaces into countably many parts with no embedding of infinite-dimensional subspaces from one partition to another. One key limitation of recommender systems is data scarcity resulting in considerable variability. Various approaches have been implemented to optimize the bias-variance equilibrium utilizing supplementary information. In particular, methods incorporating text-based document modeling have significantly improved accuracy by incorporating data from relevant sources. Nonetheless, these models may be susceptible to flooding from irrelevant data, which can worsen their performance. Furthermore, using only text-based methods overlooks other significant user behavior aspects. In response to these challenges, there's a growing need for systems integrating multiple data sources and models. In this research, we present an enhanced hybrid recommender system that integrates an advanced context-aware method and a cutting-edge collaborative filtering technique. We have developed a novel model that integrates the strengths of context-aware and collaborative filtering by combining the results of two different training methods. In particular, we combine the effects of two training methods - one using a deep learning-based neural network and another using a graph-based deep learning technique - on two distinct data sources. We have tested our model against various baseline methods, and the results demonstrate its superior performance compared to existing systems. Notably, our hybrid approach performed well across different evaluation metrics and data densities, whereas some existing hybrid systems struggled with variability. In particular, our model exhibited improved accuracy in sparse data environments and significantly outperformed other systems by a margin of up to 8.5% in diverse data conditions. In addition to these findings, we have conducted an in-depth analysis of our model's parameters and companion components, which provided further insights into their roles and reinforced the model's validity. In a real-world test, our model displayed a 24.2% increase in long-term accuracy when compared to a system that didn't consider document context. We have tested our model's robustness through various stress tests and found it to be relatively resilient to data and hyperparameter changes. Additionally, this research has significant implications for non-committal independence in matrices and various other statistical ensembles, such as Wigner's semi-circle law and heavy-tailed distributions. Furthermore, we apply our findings to study the statistical behavior of spectral measures resulting from random matrix operations such as multiplication and division. The proof of our primary outcome relies on a novel extension of non-committal independence to countable groups and a powerful theorem that links the openness of type $B$ with a particular functional equation. We believe this theorem has broad independent significance and can be used in multiple contexts. Finally, we employ our results to investigate the spectral distribution of products and quotients of independent GUE matrices and derive expressions for their density and distribution functions using a novel method. The spectral distribution also exhibits a continuous transition from a heavy-tailed power-law behavior to a gap at zero that occurs as the matrix size increases. We note that these results are highly consistent with eigenvalue behavior observed in our simulations. This concise equation encompasses the perfect gas model, is applicable to all alkali metals, and accurately predicts their behavior across a broad pressure range (up to $\sim 10^5$~Pa) and temperature range (up to $\sim 3 \cdot 10^3$~K). In inertial gauge symplectic initial condition algorithms, solving Poisson's equations for average momenta becomes particularly challenging when dealing with complex systems like numerical relativity. This difficulty is exacerbated in the presence of boundaries, where additional complications arise from truncated lattices. We propose a novel method called Average Momenta from Configurations (AMFC), which utilizes configurations instead of averages to resolve these issues. Our technique is efficient, especially for large systems, as evidenced by its successful application to the collapse of a dust cloud in the case of a single gravitational wave and two black holes. The code, which is based on pyNEURO and CTTK, has been tested in multiple tests, including one that evolved from the Looped Initial Data Problem. This method could serve as a versatile tool for symplectic initial conditions and reduce the computational costs associated with relaxing constraints. Furthermore, it is likely to be beneficial in scenarios involving multiple objects and long-term simulations. We provide the AMFC code, which is compatible with CTTK, as a package called pyAMFC, for the benefit of the relativity community. pyAMFC can be accessed at https://github.com/CTTK/AMFC_jai.19.11.21.git. Recently, online learning platforms have obtained massive datasets of student code reviews, offering considerable financial incentives to individual instructors who label these programs. To minimize costs, we propose a novel approach, pairwise iterative logits ensemble (PILE), which utilizes multiple instructors' labels to their full potential. PILE does this by generating a logit ensemble for each code review via an iterative process involving multiple rounds of pairwise instructor pairing. In each round, PILE uses one accredited instructor to re-rank the logit lists produced by another, less experienced instructor, and fine-tunes the logit lists of both instructors through a logit correction process based on the top choices made by the more experienced instructor. Notably, PILLE outperforms existing methods in terms of overall performance and financial efficiency when evaluated on a large dataset of Microsoft's Professional Developer Services, which consists of code reviews labeled by experienced software engineers. By optimizing the approach over three stages - hyperparameter settings, instructor pairing, and logit ensemble fine-tuning - our method successfully reduced waste and increased profits in a simulated dev environment. Specifically, PILLE reduced labeling time by 20.56% and increased profit by 13.61% compared to the baseline model. PILLE has also been made available as an open-source tool for automatic code review labeling. Our research demonstrates that, through targeted optimization, distillation methods like PILLE can surpass human performance and yield significant financial gains in expert-labeled datasets. In our research, we thoroughly investigate the intersection of fairness and differential privacy in federated learning, encompassing three key aspects: achieving fairness without compromising privacy, determining the optimal trade-off between privacy and fairness, and making differential privacy compatible with general fairness metrics. Our experimental findings, based on the implementation of various algorithms on MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets, support the best-in-class approach identified in our analytical analysis. Moreover, our findings shed light on the underlying dynamics of Federated Learning Differential Privacy, highlighting distinct communication periods requiring different privacy considerations. Finally, our study also sheds light on making fairness metrics compatible with differential privacy by developing a novel formulation to approximate arbitrary fairness metrics with a privacy-friendly minimum. Our future work will focus on improving NBcoded further and exploring new applications of this efficient classifier. Our future research will also involve comparing NBcoded with other existing models and providing a more in-depth analysis of the efficiency and accuracy of NBcoded. Our future work will also involve evaluating NBcoded on other types of data, such as electronic health records and text data, as well as examining the potential of utilizing NBcoded for encoding sensitive information and preserving privacy. Recent breakthroughs in artificial intelligence and machine learning have enabled algorithms to make predictions and identify patterns in complex systems, particularly within large datasets. This research examines how these algorithms can uncover universal laws governing complex phenomena, revealed through large amounts of related data, by detecting inconsistencies within that data. In physics, model discrepancies are often used to inform theory; we explore a similar approach, using predictions from these algorithms as a primary means of understanding the underlying physics of a system. This novel methodology leverages machine learning models to reveal the point at which they no longer fit the data, providing valuable insights into a system's behavior, particularly when little is known from the outset. We apply this approach to two simple systems: a particle under uniform acceleration and electromagnetic waves. By comparing algorithmic predictions to established physical models, the discrepancies can shed light on the subject's underlying physics. We find that deep learning algorithms can uncover fundamental principles, such as $F=ma$ and $E=kx$, even in the presence of limited and noisy data. Furthermore, algorithmic discrepancies can pinpoint key assumptions in physical models that were previously taken for granted, like the wave equation's assumption of constant wave speed. We hypothesize that this emerging method, which we call physico-empiricism, may enable algorithms to uncover new universal laws that have yet to be discovered in physics. Its potential applications are vast and could be used to inform policies in high-stakes domains such as weather forecasting, medicine, and self-driving cars, among many others. Unlike traditional physics, which builds upon established principles, physico-empiricism begins with data and uncovers fundamental truths, even when the underlying physics is unknown or poorly understood. We believe this approach holds immense promise for advancing our understanding of the world and its underlying laws. It is particularly well-suited to systems involving machine-generated or massive datasets, like traffic flow, social behavior, and gene expression, among many other domains. We encourage researchers to explore this novel methodology and its various applications, which we've made available on the GitHub platform. Furthermore, we've developed interactive visualizations that demonstrate the power of physico-empiricism, using state-of-the-art technologies like JupyterNotebooks and JavaScript/HTML, for a more immersive learning experience. We envision a future where algorithms and physicists collaborate to uncover new universal laws, providing a deeper understanding of the world and its underlying phenomena. In doing so, physico-empiricism may also identify inconsistencies in existing physical models, providing valuable insights and paving the way for future research

This study employs the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider to investigate the presence of hypothetical heavy, charged, long-lived particles in proton-proton collisions amounting to 139 inverse femtobarns of data collected at 13 TeV energy. The search targets particles with significantly lower ionization energy losses compared to $W$ or $Z$ bosons, and those that are slow enough to be detected by triggering on events featuring multiple tracks and high magnetic energy loss. Although its existence has been widely identified, the boson peak's features and its role in determining a material's thermodynamic properties, such as specific heat, remain poorly understood. A series of experiments in our group used advanced neutron scattering instruments to investigate the boson peak in various amorphous materials with varying thermal histories. Our analysis of the data is presented here and will be followed by a detailed discussion of the findings and their implications in a later publication. In optimization problems with multiple optimal solutions, an ideal search process would yield a diverse set of optimal solutions. Current multi-objective optimization techniques focus primarily on finding a single optimal solution. This study investigates how multi-objective optimization approaches can be modified to produce a diverse set of optimal solutions in multi-optimal problems. Additionally, we examine the relationship between solution diversity and solution distribution across the Pareto-frontier's dimensions. This analysis enables future research to target specific diversity enhancement approaches and provides insights into overall diversity achievement. Moreover, our findings are grounded by examining the optimization of 32 problems from the BBOB-2009 benchmark suite in the NODEA framework. This study reveals that multi-objective optimization processes naturally exhibit diversity, but only up to a certain point, beyond which they plateau. It becomes difficult to increase diversity further, and we propose several reasons for this phenomenon. Finally, some promising strategies to enhance diversity in multi-objective optimization processes are identified and discussed. These findings contribute to developing more effective methods to produce diverse optimal solutions in multi-objective optimization processes. At the same time, some limitations and challenges of enhancing diversity in such processes are uncovered, leaving some questions to be explored in the future. Specifically, it is unknown whether more elaborate optimization processes can produce even greater diversity, and it is also unclear how to successfully implement strategies that focus on both diversity and solution quality. Thus, some promising directions for future research are identified and highlighted. In particular, we suggest that future research could investigate more sophisticated optimization processes, such as those that incorporate artificial intelligence, to see if they can produce more diversity, and it is also proposed that future research could explore the use of deep learning to improve multi-objective optimization processes, particularly those that balance diversity and solution quality. Additionally, it is suggested that future research could involve more participants to verify the effectiveness of the strategies to enhance diversity, and it is also proposed that future research could involve examining the performance of optimization algorithms in real-world applications to see if they produce diverse optimal solutions. These are just a few of the promising directions for future research that were identified and highlighted in this study.
