The Stable Roommates problem deals with pairing a set of agents in a way that their individual preferences are satisfied. The preferences are represented as numerical values assigned to potential matchings, with higher numbers indicating stronger preferences. The goal is to create pairs (agents) such that: (1) the preference values remain positive, and (2) the preference values remain positive for any changes made. The first goal ensures stability, and the second goal ensures $\epsilon$-stability. We focus on finding whether an $\epsilon$-stable and positive-stable matching exists. The conditions under which an $\epsilon$-stable matching is guaranteed to exist were previously established with linear preferences; we expand on these results to cover additively separable preferences and prefer complete pairs. We demonstrate that an $\epsilon$-stable matching may not exist with additively separable preferences even when all preferences are symmetric and prefer complete pairs. To address this issue, we define a new concept of quasi-stable matchings, and show that an quasi-stable matching with a large enough preference margin exists. The findings on quasi-stable matchings also apply to 1-stable matchings. The complexity of checking the existence of these new stable matching types was previously unknown for sizes $n$ greater than or equal to $7$, but we show it is decidable and can be computed in polynomial time when sizes are $n$ less than or equal to $6$. A new polynomial-time algorithm for finding quasi-stable matchings when preferences are prefer complete pairs, even with additive preferences that may not be symmetric, was also developed. The research was initially presented as a conference paper at WAOA 2019. To make the findings more accessible, we have released an implementation in Python on a public repository. The code includes functions for finding quasi-stable and 1-stable matchings, as well as detecting the inexistence of these matchings, and has been used in experiments with large datasets. It also offers a command-line interface for quickly calculating these new stable matching types. The research has since been cited in multiple papers. A proposed direction for future study involves exploring quasi-stable matchings with the additional constraint of being fair. The idea of using a fair quasi-stable matching was presented as an open question. We predict it to be an important area of research in understanding how to find stable matchings that prioritize both satisfaction and equality. A microstrip-fed patch antenna designed to operate at mm-waves with broad bandwidth and a wide angle of coverage has been successfully created and tested for integration in planar arrays. The designed antenna has a significant bandwidth of 13.1%, operating between 34.1 GHz and 38.9 GHz, facilitated by the combination of a slotted microstrip patch with multiple resonances and an optimized microstrip matching circuit. Constructed using the low-cost RO3003 substrate with top and ground layers, this design accommodates simple integration with other microstrip and frontend components via top-layer microstrip coupling gap feed. The achieved wide beamwidth of 100-125 degrees is primarily due to strategically designed parasitic patches for the primary resonant frequency and inherently wide beamwidth for the second resonant frequency within the specified bandwidth, making this a highly efficient microstrip patch antenna for operation over a ground plane. The input impedance and radiation pattern observed through measured data closely agree with the simulated results. The designed antenna has exhibited maximum efficiency of 35% at 37 GHz across the specified bandwidth. Additionally, the antenna's polarization has been found to be approximately axial with minor cross-polarization due to microstrip coupling gap feed and the influence of microstrip parasites and slotted patch design. The concept of this design using a slotted microstrip antenna with multi-resonance and microstrip parasites, accompanied by broad bandwidth and wide beamwidth capabilities, offers a valuable insight for the optimization of microstrip patch antenna designs. The integration of this designed antenna into a planar array could potentially offer superior performance and efficiency in mm-wave communications. The Rojidi et al. method was used to calculate the antenna's constant of expansion, demonstrating that a design without adjustable components could still achieve reasonably good expansion constant (K_e) values of 0.093 and efficiency constant (K_eff) values of 0.93 for two different polarization configurations. The design has the potential for integration into low-cost, broad-bandwidth, wide-beamwidth microstrip patch antenna arrays operating within the 18-26 GHz frequency range with K_e ~-6 and efficiency constant (K_eff) ~0.9 for two different polarization states. The research on this design has been documented in a recent patent (US Patent 11238790). The designed antenna's operation outside the specified bandwidth may exhibit decreased efficiency and input impedance due to microstrip coupling and the influence of microstrip parasites, suggesting the need for microstrip tuning circuits to optimize performance outside the specified bandwidth. Large-scale, error-resilient quantum computing relies heavily on fault-tolerant techniques. Cross error correction, the primary method, necessitates extensive quantum circuit construction, including diverse and often redundant code preparations. Our approach utilizes reinforcement learning to create compact neural networks converting any quantum state into a desired coded version, even in the presence of cross errors. This results in reduced circuit complexity and a more efficient, compact architecture for large-scale quantum computing. Specifically, our method allows for the direct conversion between any two quantum states, an important feature for fault-tolerant computing, and our experiments show that the complexity of our circuits is substantially less than traditional constructions. Furthermore, our results indicate that the compactness of our neural networks can be scaled up without compromising functionally equivalent pairs of input and output states, an property we term state equivalency. We demonstrate significant reductions in circuit complexity, specifically a factor of ~8.3 times less gates for a qubit triple, and our results suggest an exponential decrease in circuit complexity as code size increases. Additionally, our findings suggest that the compactness of our neural networks can be scaled up without compromising their performance. A critical factor in the optimal solution to any problem involves the resources required to execute it, with optimality dependent on this wealth being adequately supplied. This concept is reflected in the wealth space, a dimensionality reduction method that compresses data from high dimensionality to a number equivalent to the amount of available wealth, thereby facilitating generalizability of supervised machine learning models when operating under constraints. When a measure of wealth within the wealth space is selected using a growth maximization strategy, this results in models capable of handling Intrinsic Rank Collapsing, a phenomenon where suboptimal features are efficiently eliminated, and optimality is achieved with limited resources. Monolithic CMOS sensors featuring small collection electrodes are advantageous due to high signal quality and low power consumption. However, these sensors are prone to radiation damage and sensitive to temperature changes. In this study, researchers explored the performance characteristics of different detector thicknesses and substrate types using the CLICTD technology, a small collection-electrode design. CLICTD was tested on 200mm wafer samples, which were then mounted on either 300um thick high-resistivity Czochralski silicon or 450um thick Teledyne Fundry silicon substrates. X-ray photons and 123GeV proton beams were used to investigate the sensors' response across various thicknesses. In addition to examining detection capabilities, researchers also investigated the charge collection efficiency and the angular response of the CLICTD technology. This study found that a thin detector region of 50um produced the best results, with a 1.5 T 1/cm region stopping power and around 25ke electron equivalent. A 125 T 1/cm region thick detector region was also investigated and showed charge collection efficiencies near 90% with a 5.4ke effective acceptance threshold. In general, the 300um Czochralski silicon substrates demonstrated better performance characteristics than the 450um Teledyne Fundry silicon substrates due to lower thermal noise and less damage from cosmic rays. A 50 T 1/cm region thick detector with a 5.4ke effective acceptance threshold was observed on the Czochralski silicon substrates, with a 1.5 T 1/cm region thick detector and an 8.1ke effective acceptance threshold on the Teledyne Fundry silicon substrates. These results indicate that a thick detector region could contribute significantly to particle identification, particularly for particles with energies above 5ke, in conditions similar to those of CLIC's first phase. In conclusion, researchers found that a 50 T 1/cm region thick detector with a 5.4ke effective acceptance threshold on the 300um Czochralski silicon substrates offered the best performance, making it an ideal choice for monolithic CMOS sensors in particle physics applications. Similarly, a 1.5 T 1/cm region thick detector and an 8.1ke effective acceptance threshold on the 450um Teledyne Fundry silicon substrates also demonstrated promising results, indicating the potential for improved particle detection in conditions beyond CLIC's first phase. Despite recent improvements, a significant barrier remains, with the ability of current high-tech ground-based telescopes limited by the ability to accurately observe through the distorted atmosphere.  Researchers have developed a groundbreaking technique known as "Fast Atmospheric Self-coherent Optics," which uses sophisticated data processing and multiple images to enhance the clarity of observed data, although this method has only been tested using computer simulations until now.  This technique has been successfully tested on a laboratory set-up, showing promising results with the ability to accurately observe through the distorted atmosphere, with the ability to reliably detect a mock planet despite the distortions.  This testing marks an important step towards incorporating fast atmospheric self-coherent optics into real-world telescopes, paving the way for future breakthroughs in planet detection and analysis.  In particular, this technology has the potential to significantly enhance the effectiveness of the upcoming Extremely Large Telescopes, making it possible to discover many more planets at closer distances, lower masses, or older ages than ever before. This research is a crucial first step towards leveraging fast atmospheric self-coherent optics and improving our ability to observe the celestial world. We provide a bi-functional correspondence between the Markov evolution of a stochastic lambda-term and the continuous-time Markov chain generated by its cut-free weak-normalisation-proof. This relation reveals a novel understanding of the random lambda-calculus as a strong lifting of the abstract-interpretation-based semantics previously introduced for the random lambda-calculus. By identifying a well-quasi-ordering on the generated Markov chains, we demonstrate the existence of a universal transition system, leading to the construction of a unique and adequate weak-distinguishability semantics for the random lambda-calculus. Furthermore, we show the equivalence between this transition system and the one generated by the abstract-interpretation-based semantics. This allows us to give a universal representation of the semantics of the random lambda-calculus. Along the way, we establish a correspondence between the generated Markov chains and the 'flow graphs' used in the abstract-interpretation-based semantics, providing evidence for the soundness of this method. Since many concrete domains for stress testing can be seen as specific sub-domains of the random lambda-calculus domain, our results can be extended to these domains as well. Eventually, we prove that the universal transition system can be approximated by an enumerable set of accelerations, leading to the construction of an optimal acceleration for the random lambda-calculus. This optimal acceleration can be applied to the general domain of stress testing and forms the core of the semantic analysis method. In the course of our research, we have also further developed and tested a prototype-based implementation of the abstract-interpretation-based method, demonstrating its practical applicability for stress testing. This tool has been successfully applied in various concrete examples and has been used to guide the development of an optimal acceleration for one of these domains. A detailed description of both the abstract-interpretation-based method and its implementation is included in this thesis as an appendix. Proximal methods can efficiently optimize non-smooth objectives across varied structural environments.  To leverage their effectiveness, we describe an algorithm combining a non-smooth stratum-wise non-negative least squares problem with a proximal gradient method, allowing for an alternative optimization procedure.  By incorporating a trust region strategy, we derive a regularization term, leading to an expression reminiscent of Newton's method.  Furthermore, our approach maintains convergence to a critical point within the feasible domain.  To illustrate the algorithm's capabilities, we apply it to a joint image processing task and a tensor regression problem emanating from a restricted negative mass model in computational neuroscience.  The results showcase its ability to handle non-differentiable objectives while exploiting structural information to enhance convergence performance.  The developed approach provides a versatile framework for analyzing acoustic scenes and data interpretation in auditory neuroscience.  Furthermore, its success in real-world domains not commonly associated with non-smooth optimization highlights the diversity of applications supported by proximal optimization techniques.  Based on theoretical insights gained from our findings, we recommend the incorporation of proximal optimization as a practical tool for tackling acoustic analysis and related biomedical problems. Several local authorities face challenges in deploying smart infrastructure for road condition monitoring due to the substantial time and financial commitments involved. Recent advances in deep learning have yielded promising results for road damage detection, yet most of these studies rely on specific, country-based datasets. This research aims to address the inherent difficulties and limitations of single-country approaches by developing a transferable, adaptable solution for multiple countries. Our solution involves designing a new, deep learning-based framework with adjustable, transferable components to accommodate diverse image characteristics and damage patterns. This framework is tested on datasets from India and Indonesia to determine the optimal approach for transferring knowledge and adapting the model to new, unseen environments. Our results demonstrate that our framework can significantly enhance damage detection accuracy in countries without sufficient data by leveraging knowledge from more advanced, well-established countries. Additionally, our model can easily adjust to new data by incorporating it in an ensemble training method that further improves performance. These findings showcase the potential for using transfer learning to build a versatile, efficient, and accurate road damage detection system that can be rapidly deployed and adapted to various settings worldwide with minimal adjustments. The primary objective is to identify the most compact association rules that occur frequently within the data. Achieving this involves finding the smallest number of conditions that can generate these rules through implication deduction. Individuals who interact with the police and courts are more likely to experience mental health difficulties and, in the case of convictions, are compelled to undergo treatment for distress.  This treatment, though intended to be therapeutic, may be felt as coercive, potentially hindering individuals from seeking help voluntarily.  Concerns surrounding the use of required therapy by the state could further exacerbate the stigma associated with mental illness.  The impact of compelled therapy on its effectiveness and overall well-being remains unclear, particularly in terms of its long-term effects and the potential for harm caused by the loss of trust between the state and its citizens.  This study investigates how required therapy, either as a condition of their sentence, affects the mental health of convicted individuals by examining the effect of exposure to forced therapy on their symptoms of depression and anxiety.  To conduct this research, data from the National Crime Victimization Survey from 2008 to 2017 was used, with focused analysis on individuals who had interacted with the criminal justice system and were also diagnosed with depression or anxiety.  The findings reveal that exposure to forced therapy results in a statistically significant and long-term increase in the symptoms of depression and anxiety.  This effect is observed to persist even after controlling for factors such as prior therapy and medication use.  The evidence suggests that compelled therapy may not only fail to improve but actually worsen mental health, suggesting a need for alternative, more voluntary post-conviction treatment systems that prioritize the trust and consent between the state and its citizens.  Furthermore, it is crucial that any therapy required by the state is designed to address the coercive element and develops a patient-centered approach that respects autonomy and the need for informed consent.  Through this research, we aim to contribute to a critical discussion on the use of compelled therapy within the criminal justice system and its potential to harm mental health, particularly when it undermines the delicate balance of trust between the state and its citizens.  This research offers a unique perspective on the issue by examining how required therapy, though intended to be therapeutic, could actually increase depression and anxiety symptoms in convicted individuals, even in the long term.  The study provides empirical evidence that compelled therapy may not only fail to improve mental health but actually worsen it, and suggests that any therapy required by the state should prioritize its consent and trustworthiness to address its coercive element and develop a patient-centered approach. A proposed novel approach leverages autonomous UAVs collecting passive spectrum data at various locations to efficiently estimate the radio map.  A UAV's movement between gathering points is managed using a near-optimal route planner.  A radio map estimation technique, which trades off exploration and exploitation, is also designed.  A real-time radio map updating method enables adaptive operation without the need for prior channel parameter estimation.  A mathematical analysis and simulations validate the feasibility and effectiveness of this approach, particularly in scenarios with restricted UAV access and channel variation over time.  A possible solution to these challenges could be implementing a dual-scale navigation system, which is explored in future research. A individual verification system utilizes distinctive human characteristics, such as voice, face, and fingerprints, to create a unique identity profile. This identification method is known as unimodal individual verification. However, this method may encounter problems with security risks and complications arising from feature extraction difficulties or system design flaws. To address these challenges, a new approach called multimodal individual verification utilizes combinations of unimodal systems to enhance the robustness of identification methods. Although multimodal verification offers improved robustness, its performance can still be hindered by problems such as verification difficulty, definition ambiguity, and overlapping identification categories. To resolve these issues, this research aims to develop an advanced verification system that utilizes combined audio-visual-thermal modalities and applies a complex classifier, specifically the attention-based deep learning approach. The proposed system was tested using the OuluCSDB database and the experimental results indicate significant improvements in our approach, particularly in challenging conditions. Moreover, this paper includes comparisons with established deep learning methods, such as the CoAttNet, PPAttNet, PAM, DPN, and Siamese networks, to demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed system. The overall objective of this research is to develop a robust identification system capable of handling complex problems and unsupervised identification processes. The proposed model shows promising results in these areas, particularly in comparison with unimodal and existing multimodal verification systems. Notably, the proposed method outperforms other deep learning methods by achieving a 93.6% verification rate at a 0 false accept rate (FRR) using the OuluCSDB database, highlighting its potential for real-world individual verification applications. The main research contributions of this research can be summarized as follows: (i) the development of a new multimodal verification system using audio-visual-thermal modalities, (ii) employment of the attention-based deep learning approach, and (iii) testing and evaluation of the system using a widely used database and a range of unimodal and multimodal verification methods. The source code for this research has been made available on GitHub for the purpose of facilitating future work and applications. Consider a parametric family of distributions defined by a vector of parameters $\theta$ and an unknown distribution $\Pi$ over a finite set $\Lambda$ of possible parameters. We want to estimate the average parameter, denoted $\Pi(\theta)$, based on a sample of size $n$ from a mixture of distributions given by $\Pi(\theta)=\frac{\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda}\theta\lambda}{N(\theta)}$, where $N(\theta)=\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda}\frac{1}{\lambda}$. This research develops methods for estimating $\Pi(\theta)$ and its components, $\lambda/\sqrt{N(\theta)}$, in the context of known finite mixtures using conventional empirical estimation techniques. We examine the statistical efficiency of these estimators and provide alternative estimators with higher efficiency that are specific to certain types of parameter combinations, along with the efficiency gains. A method called the multiple-fold empirical distribution function estimator is introduced to study the behavior of these estimators and allows for an empirical central limit theorem to be established. This research also addresses estimation challenges related to sampling from a mixture distribution, including a free-kernel approach that provides more accurate results than traditional methods for estimating parameters and kernel densities. Simulation experiments are conducted to demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed methods. Finally, this research includes a practical application to estimate technical indicators of stock market activity using data from the Random Walk hypothesis. A significant outcome of this research is the implementation of a method that allows for non-parametric estimation of the average price movement of stocks over a specified period of time. This new method combines price data with volume data to produce more accurate estimates of stock behavior. A related idea called the Random Walk Minimum Energy Surface has been developed, along with its empirical version. Both concepts have been used to analyze the Random Walk hypothesis and the Efficient Market hypothesis, along with providing independent support for these theories through non-parametric analysis. This research also includes the publication of a computer program in R that allows users to estimate the parameters and kernel densities of a mixture distribution. A demonstration of how to use this program is included in the document. This research includes numerous examples of its utility, along with the analysis of technical indicators and Random Walk patterns in the S&P 500 index. A significant outcome of this research is the implementation of a method called the Component-wise Empirical Distribution Function estimator. Recent studies employing Gaia EDR3 data have revealed numerous stellar filaments in the Milky Way, which are thought to be young star clusters still in the process of forming.  A more in-depth analysis of these structures, however, reveals that they are largely comprised of scattered, older stars with minimal young stars.  Through an examination of various properties, it becomes evident that these "filaments" possess different characteristics than true young star clusters.  Furthermore, it appears that these structures tend to have higher concentrations of red giant stars.  A possible explanation for these findings is that the Gaia astrometric errors, combined with the crowding of sources, greatly exacerbate the false positive rate for filament identification.  As a result, further research using higher-resolution data is needed to accurately pinpoint true stellar filaments and study their composition.  Prior assumptions about the relatively constant age of these structures in filaments also need re-evaluating, with some potentially consisting of sources up to 1 billion years old.  Furthermore, it becomes evident that these structures do not possess unique chemical signatures after all.  Through additional research, it is hoped that more about the mysterious stellar filaments can be uncovered.

Current studies view visual compatibility as a straightforward'match' or'mismatch' classification problem, where each garment item is labeled as entirely compatible or incompatible. Yet, this simplistic approach is impractical for real-world Outfit Maker apps where users must identify which specific items might clash with their created outfits. To address this limitation, we introduce the Visual InCompatibility TransformR (VICTOR) model, the first to accurately identify individual items' compatibility. By redefining visual compatibility as a comparative output, we leverage the strength of pre-trained Transformer models, combining this with proprietary contrastive learning techniques tailored to fashion data. Experimental evaluations demonstrate the exceptional performance of our VICTOR model, showcasing its ability to correctly predict human-assigned compatibility scores for an independent test set with high precision. Moreover, our model is robust in its predictions, even when outfit compositions are altered. To facilitate future research, we also make our fashion-centric pre-trained model available, alongside our full code and demonstration video at the provided link. This model can now be utilized to generate more accurate visual outcomes by selecting only compatible garment items in real-time, enhancing the overall quality of output sequences. With its exceptional efficacy established, our solution has the potential to support and transform the fashion industry, enabling the creation of more sophisticated Outfit Maker tools. These tools can then utilize our model to produce stunning and visually appealing outfits, enhancing user experience and engagement. In our analysis, we validate the diverse range of fashion expertise incorporated by the model, showing its ability to learn and incorporate various fashion principles, including accessory usage, to produce highly compatible outfit compositions. Through an in-depth examination of its predictions, we also gain insight into the model's understanding of visual compatibility, revealing its ability to learn and apply complex, nuanced principles governing compatible outfit configurations. These principles, such as matching jacket and shirt colors, are consistently predicted with high accuracy, as well as learning to identify compatible outfit compositions, despite the limited availability of colored fashion images in the training dataset. To further illustrate the capabilities of our model, an online demo is also provided, demonstrating its ability to dynamically filter and generate compatible outfit compositions in real-time. As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, the synchronization issue becomes more prominent. Our proposed solution, using a distributed gradient buffer and asynchronous aggregation, addresses this challenge without requiring devices to be online at the same time. By allowing devices to update their local gradients independently, even when other devices are offline or disconnected, and merging the gradients from all connected devices at the server, we maintain the same convergence rate as if all devices were synchronized. Notably, this method introduces no new bandwidth costs, aside from communication already occurring, and eliminates the need for devices to be evenly connected or the server to be reliable. Our theoretical analysis and experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of this approach, using both synthetic data and real-world scenarios involving a variety of devices. Specifically, our experiments with the LeNet5 model on the CIFAR10 dataset show that the internal aggregation process can reduce communication rounds by up to 15 times, and even more so if we factor in the effects of variable network latency. Additionally, we found that the latency effects can further limit communication efficiency by up to 2 times. Given these findings, we recommend implementing the buffered asynchronous aggregation approach in real-world federated learning systems, especially those involving large networks and devices requiring different update frequencies. Our code is publicly available, having been validated in various scenarios. In the future, we plan to expand on this research by exploring its applications in other domains and protocols, such as federated data science. Further investigation is also needed to explicitly analyze the effects of different latency patterns on the convergence rate. Potential areas of study include the correlation between network delays and the optimal gradient buffer size, and the interaction between the gradient buffer and local model design, particularly regarding when to update models and communicate them to the server. Another possible direction is to examine the feasibility of using more sophisticated aggregation methods, like the distributed averaging algorithm, in conjunction with the proposed approach. It is also worthy of further exploration whether the proposed solution can be adapted for other federated learning use cases, such as federated learning with specific device groups or user involvement patterns. By delving into these research questions, we aim to further refine our proposed solution and make significant contributions to the field of federated learning. This research focuses on developing effective techniques to estimate a nonparametric conditional expectation operator, specifically $\mathbb{E}[Y|X=x]$, based on independent and identically distributed data pairs, $(X_i,Y_i)$, under a finite second moment for $Y$ given $X$. We explore both a direct estimation approach and an indirect approach involving kernel ridge regression. The initial method employs a weighted least-squares technique within a kernel framework that can be efficiently estimated without parametric assumptions. The alternative approach, employing kernel ridge regression, estimates a universal least-squares projector even though it may involve a more complex estimation method. Both techniques converge at a rate of $n^{-4/(4+k)}$, which is in line with nonparametric estimation trends, despite initial concerns suggesting a slower convergence rate due to the influence of the kernel's width. We present fully functional software programs in MATLAB and Python to facilitate replication of the results presented in this research. Furthermore, we provide comprehensive evidence and analysis on the performance of these estimation methods, including a proof examining the performance of kernel ridge regression and a preliminary investigation into the potential benefits of incorporating Markov chain Monte Carlo techniques into the analysis. This leads to the development of a novel method, Markov chain kernel ridge regression, which exhibits improved performance and accurate estimation at a rate of $n^{-4/(4+2)}$, making it a highly effective tool for applying machine learning techniques to conditional expectation estimation projects. A formal theoretical analysis for the first time explains why this method demonstrates better performance and justifies the widespread adoption of Markov chain Monte Carlo techniques in nonparametric estimation projects. Additionally, we present a proof demonstrating that incorporating Markov chain Monte Carlo techniques significantly reduces the influence of the kernel's width, which is a key performance metric, by a factor of four, thereby greatly improving the efficiency of this method. This research presents the first successful application of Markov chain Monte Carlo techniques in nonparametric estimation projects, along with a comprehensive evaluation of the performance of this method and its extension to a broad family of Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithms, along with a proof providing a general upper limit on the rate of convergence for this broad class of algorithms. The recent surge in Deep Learning based Knowledge Graph Embedding (KGE) techniques has made traditional link prediction models seem antiquated.  Despite this perception, our empirical findings indicate that contemporary link prediction models using static models outperform those using KGEs on temporal knowledge graphs.  We present a novel approach called TimeKG2Vec which combines the benefits of both static models and KGEs, ultimately yielding better performance.  Additionally, we conducted an in-depth analysis of hyperparameters, model selection, and robustness across various metrics, showcasing the effectiveness of static models in link prediction.  We have made the code available for reproduction of our results at https://github.com/jbmeier/TimeKG2Vec.  Our study reveals that static models remain a viable choice for knowledge graph completion tasks.  We observe improvements in F1 score of up to 25% and MPE of up to 0.7 for certain settings, particularly in graphs with time-sensitive edge information.  Notably, our models exhibit exceptional recall rates on head-entity prediction, outperforming embeddings-based methods by as much as 20%.  We attribute the success of static models to their ability to effectively model time-based relationships, as evidenced by the substantial declines (up to 30%) in F1 score when the time component is removed.  We conclude that static models bring a beneficial perspective to the field of link prediction and embedding techniques.  We envision them being utilized in applications involving graph navigation and recommendation systems, enhancing the understanding of graph dynamics and structure.  Furthermore, static models can facilitate the explanation and interpretability of model behavior through examining weight adjustments over time. In this research, we have examined the breakdown of a heavy heavy quark (specifically, the charm or bottom quark) in a strong magnetic field, taking into account its effects on the light and heavy flavors. Using a heavy-dense lagrangian and assuming a heavy quark mass that is much greater than the magnetic field strength, we have derived the propagator of a heavy quark in a magnetic field and incorporated an asymptotic expansion up to the sixth power of the magnetization. This approach allows us to analyze the anisotropic structure of heavy quark disintegration in a magnetic field through its self-energy and diffusion equations. Our findings indicate that in the case of heavy quark disintegration, magnetic field effects are minimal at very high magnetization levels (order $m_Q^2$ or higher), but significantly impact the process at lower magnetization levels (order $s \ll m_Q^2$). A key observation is that when the magnetic field is split into two components (parallel and perpendicular directions), magnetic field effects are prominent only in the parallel direction. This is particularly noticeable in the diffusion equation, where the anisotropic part is much greater in one direction than the other. Our research thus demonstrates that in the context of heavy quark disintegration, magnetic field effects are significant at lower energies and primarily manifest as an increase in diffusion in the direction parallel to the magnetic field. This finding is particularly notable in heavy quark physics and is the first instance where magnetic field effects have been shown to alter diffusion in this realm. Furthermore, our research reveals that in the limit of very high magnetization (order $m_Q^2$ or higher), magnetic field effects are minimal and the anisotropic structure of heavy quark disintegration is largely driven by differences in mass between heavy and light flavors. This is remarkable as it indicates that in high-energy scenarios, magnetic field effects are insignificant and the anisotropic structure of heavy quark disintegration is primarily driven by mass differences. Finally, our research also underscores the significance of incorporating higher-order terms (order $1/m_Q^6$ and higher) in the propagator to accurately capture magnetic field effects, particularly at lower energies. In fact, our research demonstrates that incorporating these higher-order terms is essential for capturing the anisotropic diffusion of heavy quarks in magnetic fields, especially at lower energies. Detecting complex multifrequency microwave (MW) electric fields is difficult 
due to interference from overlapping signals. Research using Rydberg atoms 
recognizes MW patterns via atomic responses that vary depending on the frequency 
and intensity. Our study combines this principle with a deep learning algorithm, 
leveraging its ability to interpret complex patterns. By training a Rydberg atom 
network on a series of discrete frequencies, we've improved the recognition of 
continuous spectra containing multiple signals. Our findings demonstrate that 
rydberg atoms can be employed in the detection of MW fields with intricate 
patterns. Additionally, we've explored the feasibility of transferring learning 
between Rydberg-based neural networks trained on distinct frequency ranges. Our 
results indicate that by utilizing Rydberg atoms at different hyperfine levels, 
deep learning can facilitate the recognition of MW fields with unfamiliar 
frequencies. These breakthroughs may enable the development of a Rydberg-based 
portable device capable of sensing MW fields, including those used in atomic 
clocks and quantum computing systems. Our study provides a foundation for deep 
learning applications in quantum and fundamental physics research. Our work is the 
first to apply transfer learning to Rydberg multifold microwave recognition.

UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, is characterized by an unusually high surface brightness disk. Using the KORCA integral field unit, we examined the Hα emission and Reynolds stress in a major star-forming region within the galaxy. Our analysis revealed high Reynolds stress levels, equivalent to several hundred km²/s, which are likely the primary force driving gas transport and circulation in the disk. Although a strong spiral pattern in the Hα emission map suggests the presence of a stellar bar, the Hα distribution does not reveal a clear bar shape. Most of the star-forming activity is concentrated at the heart of the galaxy, and the high ionization energy in the central region may indicate a significant contribution from ascendant shocks. Moreover, the strong 400 km/s velocity gradient in the north-south direction further confirms the presence of a weak fan-like structure. It is possible that the stable disk pattern of UGC 8839 is a rare phenomenon in galaxies with low surface brightness. To explore this idea, we compared our findings to a neighboring galaxy, UGC 8851, which has a similar orientation but a more normal spiral galaxy appearance. A comparison of their properties revealed a significant difference in surface brightness and color maps, particularly a more pronounced blue color in UGC 8839, which is likely the result of their different interaction with a nearby companion galaxy. However, a more in-depth analysis of their stability is needed to confirm the relationship between hyper-stable disk property and low surface brightness in galaxies. To facilitate further research, we have constructed a near-infrared surface brightness map for 52 spiral galaxies, which can be accessed through the GALEC database at http://www.astro.ufl.edu/∼dprice/galec.html. This project is a contribution to the GALEC project, and we are planning to publish the findings in a series of research papers. To summarize, our analysis of UGC 8839 reveals a unique galaxy with extraordinary properties, and our comparison with fellow spiral galaxies using the Hα distribution and Reynolds stress suggests that the hyper-stable disk phenomenon is an important factor in understanding their behavior. This research has significant implications for modeling galaxy evolution, particularly the role of Reynolds stress in gas transport and the formation of star-forming regions. Further study of UGC 8839 and similar galaxies is essential to unravel the underlying physical processes in their stable disk patterns. To this end, we have made the data available through the GALEC database at http://www.astro.ufl.edu

Recent breakthroughs in sound design from visual patterns hold great promise for creating immersive audio experiences. Yet, the current sound generation methods lack stability, producing low-quality sound in roughly half of all cases. To address this issue, we propose VSDS-Synthesizer, a reliable deep model that accurately extracts sound data from visually compelling input. By utilizing a well-designed residual network, VSDS-Synthesizer produces high-fidelity sound data at a resolution of 44 kHz within a timeframe of 1 second. Recurrent Neural Networks have become a crucial tool for handling sequential data in the field of Deep Learning. Unlike traditional neural networks, which rely on individual, non-repeating input layers, RNNs can handle variable sequence lengths containing numerous input vectors. Although versatile, RNNs face challenges with gradient vanishing problems during backpropagation. To address this issue, architectures such as Unfold and Residual have been developed. Another solution, proposed by Xavier Gaudreau, involves leveraging the structure of temporal data using temporal analysis techniques from signal processing and control theory. By employing analysis tools, features extraction can be performed, eliminating the need for manual feature engineering. Ultimately, combining these techniques holds potential for groundbreaking applications in deep learning. This paper presents a comprehensive study on RNNs, their variants and associated challenges, providing an accessible entry point for students and practitioners to engage with this topic. To conclude, a comprehensive evaluation of RNN-based methods on 12 real-world tasks is performed, highlighting the performance of individual techniques and their combinations. Using an open-source library for hyperparameter tuning, an optimal set of parameters is found and compared with existing baseline results to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed techniques. Finally, an open-source repository containing all code examples, along with a standardized dataset, is made available for further study. This work aims to contribute to the field of RNN-based learning by providing accessible insights, with the ultimate goal of promoting research in this area. While this study may lack original research contributions, it aims to facilitate learning and promote exploration in RNN-based learning. This manuscript is an extension of the author's master's thesis, presented at CBMI 2021 and MIC 2021 conferences. This document is tailored for computer science audiences, with a focus on promoting research in RNN-based learning. This study is comprised of six sections, commencing with an introduction and a concise review of RNN-based learning, followed by an examination of techniques and code examples, a comprehensive evaluation of hyperparameters, and finally, conclusions and future work along with publicly accessible resources. Achieving a balance between mitigating the health effects and controlling the economic impact of a pandemic is a daunting task.  Identifying the optimal timing of measures to limit the spread of the pandemic and minimize both health costs and economic losses is a complex problem.  We approached this challenge by modeling the number of new infections using a time-varying reproduction number (R(t)), which varies over time in response to mitigation measures.  By applying numerical techniques to a practical model, we found that a delayed response typically results in more deaths and severe economic hardship.  We observed a critical window of opportunity before the peak of infections, known as the critical leading period, where the loss function increases rapidly.  Our study also revealed that the optimal time to implement measures may occur earlier than the critical leading period if considering only the immediate costs and benefits.  This leads to an unintended "tipping" effect when the most effective measure is switched from public health interventions to economic relaxations or vice versa.  Furthermore, our results show that the widely accepted average infection rate model yields the same solutions as the more sophisticated age-structured model.  These findings are applicable to any pandemic scenario represented by the SEIR model.  Our research highlights the significance of finding the optimal critical leading period to guide pandemic mitigation strategies.  As such, our work provides a framework for policymakers to make data-driven decisions, informed by the unique characteristics of the pandemic, to balance health and economic outcomes.
  Specifically, our findings imply that any delay in implementing measures leads to both increased deaths and severe economic losses.  Furthermore, we observed that the most effective approach may often require action well in advance of the peak of infections.  Our research also suggests that public health interventions tend to be more cost-effective than economic relaxations.  Our solutions are applicable to any pandemic model described by the SEIR framework and we observed particular features in our specific pandemic model that provide insights for pandemic mitigation strategies.  Furthermore, our work highlights the importance of the critical leading period to guide pandemic mitigation strategies.  Our research provides a framework for researchers and policymakers to make decisions, informed by the unique characteristics of the pandemic, to balance health and economic outcomes.  Our findings also emphasize the need to consider both health and economic outcomes and the tailored approach to pandemic measures depending on the transmission rate.  Our research also provides a new perspective on the decision-making criteria that are traditionally based on the average infection rate model.  Our study also highlights the differing views of experts on the critical leading period and the necessary mitigation measures.

This study provides an in-depth examination of how high pressure influences the anomalous Hall effect in Mn$_3$Sn, an antiferromagnetic compound with a triangular structure. Theoretical models predict that when exposed to pressure, Mn$_3$Sn may transition into a hexagonal structure, leading to increased pressure-dependent variations in its anomalous Hall effect. Our experimental findings, however, reveal that the anomalous Hall effect in Mn$_3$Sn undergoes a significant increase in response to pressure, rather than a decline as expected. Through a combination of experimental and computational investigations, we demonstrate that this enhancement arises from a pressure-induced change in the material's electronic properties at the Fermi level, attributed to a spin-orbit enhanced contribution. The internal pressures within Mn$_3$Sn can be mimicked by varying the composition of Mn$_3$Sn$_{1+x}$ where x represents excess Sn content ($x = 0.07$), resulting in a remarkable correlation. The material's anomalous Hall effect can thus be effectively modulated by regulating the interatomic distances through pressure or composition, presenting a novel strategy for controlling this phenomenon. Our study provides valuable insights into how Mn$_3$Sn's anomalous Hall effect responds to changes in its material structure. The predicted behavior in Mn$_3$Sn may also present a compelling opportunity to study spin-orbit entanglement in a wide class of materials exhibiting similar magnetic and electronic properties. The generalization of these findings could lead to the discovery of new materials exhibiting anomalous Hall effect, as well as new principles governing superconductivity and magnetism. The potential applications of our research include the development of more efficient electric motors, advanced sensors, and magnetic storage technologies. The in-depth analysis of our data as well as theoretical calculations presented here demonstrate that a deep understanding of how materials respond to pressure can reveal novel and practical functions that were previously unknown. Furthermore, our research may pave the way for the discovery of other amazing properties of materials that we currently know nothing about. The study provides a comprehensive analysis of Mn$_3$Sn's Anomalous Hall effect, as well as its magnetic and electronic properties, providing a wealth of information that could be useful in the development of new magnetic materials. We also present a series of interesting phenomena that result from the coexistence of superconductivity, ferromagnetism, and anomalous Hall effect in Mn$_3$Sn. The material's complex behavior presents a challenging problem for physicists, but also offers the potential for groundbreaking discoveries in materials science

Bill Thurston initially found that the Euler characteristic of a tight contact structure on a given three-manifold cannot drop below a certain lower limit. Subsequent work by David Gabai and David Meyer discovered that there is a similar lower limit for the Euler characteristic of transverse singularities in three-manifolds. David Cooper and David Long later proved that the Euler characteristic of a tight contact structure on a three-manifold cannot be greater than a upper limit. We present here a new proof that combines these earlier results of Cooper and Long with further findings of Daniel Mathieu, establishing that the Euler characteristic of a tight contact structure on a three-manifold satisfies a specific inequality. The relationship between the Euler characteristic of a tight contact structure and the Thurston norm supports this inequality. Nonetheless, research has uncovered a problem known as state distribution shift, where agents excessively focus on predicting the cause of movements rather than the current situation. We propose employing mutual information as a penalty to compel agents to utilize sensory input more thoroughly, thereby preventing over-reliance on prediction. The proposed method possesses considerable advantages: it necessitates no additional training parameters, no data can be leaked, and no manual input is required. Experiments on the NYU-VS dataset for visual navigation demonstrate that the proposed method enhances performance and prevents vision deterioration. Moreover, our method displays more realistic and practical decision-making compared to the standard actor-critic model. Our research is an initial effort to apply mutual information as a penalty in deep reinforcement learning and has considerable potential for extension to other areas of this emerging field. In the process, we introduce a category involving a specific kind of matrix action and prove that brackets within this context follow certain fundamental properties. Within the framework of 2D Kronik-Hubbard model, our investigation focuses on exploring the response of topological insulators to the introduction of defects. Through both analytical and numerical methods, we examine the impact of various types of defects, including those that alter the Rashba SOC strength, magnetic field strength, and chemical potential, on the topological properties of the system as per the Thouless criterion. Furthermore, we find in the majority of cases that the system maintains its topological attributes even in the presence of defects, with the exception of magnetic field defects which can transform a topological insulator into a topological insulator of opposing type, and Rashba SOC defects raising the topological gap in p-doped cases. Additionally, we discover that magnetic defects can transform a topological insulator into a metal, and reduce the topological gap in n-doped cases. Lastly, we find through mean-field calculations that Hubbard interactions introduce a small topological gap in the system, and have the potential to convert a topological insulator into a topological insulator of opposing type when the system is p-doped. These findings indicate that the loss or modification of topological properties in topological insulators due to defects, particularly magnetic defects, should not be underestimated, and highlight the necessity of protecting both Rashba SOC and magnetic stability to maintain the topological properties of the system. Lastly, we propose that these defects could serve as a potential mechanism for activating a topological insulator's surface state at a finite rate. This study may pave the way for an innovative strategy for generating terahertz sources, and promoting the integration of topological insulators in spintronics and phototonics systems. When a robot's work environment is hard to reach or dangerous for human workers, the task becomes even more challenging due to physical constraints. For tasks like surgery or pick-and-place operations, it's not just the robot's reach that's a concern, but also its manipulability, which measures its ability to perform tasks efficiently. To ensure a smooth handover between human and robot tasks, we need to understand how to transfer manipulability information. This information is essential for determining the feasibility of tasks and controlling robot movements. Although there are established methods for transferring point clouds and poses between humans and robots, these methods don't take into account the complex structure of manipulability. This research, therefore, focuses on developing an approach to transfer manipulability information from humans to robots. This involves converting manipulability into a compatible 3D representation to match the robot's structure. To achieve this, we're using a new method to combine and align this representation with the robot's manipulability sphere. This method leverages parallel transport to move manipulability features from the human's to the robot's coordinate system. As a by-product, we've also developed improved variants of the ICPT algorithm, which enhance point cloud and pose matching by incorporating manifold constraints, especially in difficult conditions. These new variants are used in transferring manipulability information and have been successfully tested in complex simulations and real-world experiments. The approach developed in this research is evaluated by mapping human manipulability to the robot's manipulability sphere in tasks such as surgery and pick-and-place operations. This evaluation highlights the challenges of growing the robot's manipulability sphere to match the task requirements. As a result, we've developed a new task-dependent metric for evaluating robot manipulability. This new approach successfully transfers human manipulability to the robot's manipulability sphere, allowing for improved robot arm movements and simulations of complex tasks. Additionally, we've confirmed that our ICPT variants outperform established algorithms in pose estimation and 3D structure matching tasks. This includes projects like PCL's Point Registry, which uses ICPT for structure alignment. This success has further validated the feasibility of transferring manipulability information and using it in tasks and simulations. To study Higgs boson pair production, we employed the matrix element method on specific event data from the Higgs boson decay $\textrm{HH} \to \textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$. Using complete matrix elements, we calculated the event weights for Higgs boson pair events and events from standard two-body production, then sorted them by their corresponding Q-values in ascending order. Following this, we removed events with negative weights. Our results demonstrated that the event selection technique retained more than 90% of Higgs boson pair events while eliminating over 99% of events from standard two-body production. Furthermore, we investigated the impact of the event selection on the $\textrm{HH} \to \textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ signal and background contributions under the standard two-body production assumption. Our findings indicated that the event selection maintained 80% of the Higgs boson pair signal and reduced the two-body production contribution by over two orders of magnitude. We also found that the event selection enhanced the $\textrm{HH} \to \textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ signal significance by a factor of 25. Additionally, we calculated the branching ratio for the Higgs boson decaying into bottom-quark pairs as a function of the Higgs boson pair mass, and found it to be in agreement with predictions. Our findings also demonstrated that the Higgs boson pair branching ratio exhibits minimal dependence on the Higgs boson mass within the range of 120 GeV to 250 GeV. We have proposed an improved analysis technique that utilizes the event yields of four jets and two leptons to distinguish Higgs boson pair events from standard two-body production, leading to a significant enhancement of the Higgs boson pair signal by a factor of 8 compared to current techniques. A novel method is introduced for training single-view 3D object pose estimation models, utilizing unstructured, 'in-the-wild' video footage where objects are rotated. These scenes are commonly encountered and can be easily gathered (e.g. cars navigating roundabouts), yet existing methods are ineffective in learning from such content. Our approach employs a turntable detection algorithm to identify and isolate the rotation events within this type of footage, using these events to train a pose estimation model. This model's performance surpasses current standards when evaluated on multiple datasets, further highlighting the potential of these rotating scenes by showing that the same data can simultaneously train an object detection model and a pose estimation model that excels at novel views. Our method and turntable detection algorithm are made available for public use. Additionally, an object-oriented dataset and a new benchmark were created for the community to utilize. These resources are specifically designed to facilitate research into the automatic recognition of objects and their poses, supporting the development of more robust and generalizable models through the use of unstructured video footage. Our method and these new resources are intended to enhance the field of 3D pose estimation and ultimately contribute to the creation of more resilient self-driving vehicle systems. Experimental results indicate that the models trained with our approach are more resilient to novel views, as demonstrated by an accompanying video. Our method was inspired by a simple, informal observation of how the environment influences deep learning models, particularly those pre-trained on image data, as described in the introduction of the paper. These influences can also be seen in other benchmarks, such as the PoseIndo dataset, which was created based on these observations and is complementary to our approach and existing benchmarks. While it was not the primary focus of our research, our analysis also yields insights into action recognition and suggest ways in which future studies could utilize these insights. Firstly, two object-oriented datasets were created with varying levels of annotation to address the challenge of how to train a pose estimation model when only little is known about the objects. One of these datasets, the Accidental Turntables dataset, consists of highly annotated images from studio settings and was used to establish a baseline for 3D pose estimation models. The other dataset, Object #X, consists of images with limited annotations and can serve as a benchmark for detecting objects and estimating their poses. Secondly, we identified that existing 3D pose estimation models perform better on rotations along one axis but struggle with other types of rotation, leading us to propose the Rotated Pose Estimation (RoPE) benchmark. Despite extensive promotion, a substantial number of people still resist COVID-19 vaccination. Recent studies indicate that social media platforms play a significant role in disseminating anti-vaccination information, largely fueled by misinformation campaigns. This study aims to analyze Twitter discourse and detect anti-vaccination views, specifically identifying tweets that promote prevalent misinformation leading to vaccine rejection. We examined neighboring tweets that expressed opposite sentiments, examining acceptance or rejection responses to such misinformation. Our results show that, on average, 44% of tweets rejecting the vaccine cite one or more prevailing misinformation types. Furthermore, nearly all vaccine-rejection tweets (99%) express either an anti-science or conspiracy-oriented sentiment. Additionally, we discovered that Twitter users often respond to pro-vaccine tweets with rejection responses that frequently incorporate the same misinformation types found in initial vaccine-rejection tweets. Our proposed framework and data analytics methodology contribute to the development of distinct short-text and user behavior classifiers, yielding top-classified accuracies of 93.46% for acceptance and 87.91% for rejection, as well as success rates of 0.846 for user classification and 0.814 for misinformation classification. Our results offer actionable insights for anti-disinformation campaigns, highlighting the influence of a limited number of misinformation types in shaping vaccine-rejection discourse on Twitter, as well as the utility of user-generated text contributions in distinguishing acceptance and rejection attitudes. Moreover, we provide unique perspectives on Twitter users through our proposed extractor module. Our research demonstrates that short, granular tweets hold significant predictive value for understanding complex attitudes toward COVID-19 vaccination. Ultimately, this study facilitates the utilization of social media data in refining public health policy and anti-disinformation campaigns by deepening our understanding of the intricate, multifaceted nature of vaccine-rejection discourse on Twitter. We demonstrate in this study that it is feasible to produce isolated attosecond pulses using a natural plasma in a gas medium through a laser-matter interaction that generates high-energy harmonics. This method has the advantages of high efficiency and a broad spectral range, without the necessity of sophisticated and costly experimental setups. We have successfully generated attosecond pulses in a laboratory setting, utilizing a simple and affordable experimental design that incorporates a laser pulse with a long wavelength and low energy density, thereby preventing the creation of hot electrons and nonlinear laser-matter interaction. This approach produces pulses with a duration of approximately 160 attoseconds, a peak power of over 1 gigawatt, and a coherent energy of about 5 nanojoules. We have also developed a theoretical model based on the spatial propagation equation of optical pulses to analyze the pulse duration, and found that it is feasible to produce pulses shorter than 160 attoseconds through a laser pulse with a duration of about six cycles. This research paves the way for the development of a compact, high-energy attosecond source that could revolutionize the field by enabling the observation of electronic motion at the atomic level. Furthermore, we have explored the parameters of our natural plasma-based attosecond source, estimating that it is technically feasible to achieve a pulse duration of around 160 attoseconds using a laser pulse with a duration of six cycles, a spectral range extending from 2 to 12 electron volts, and a high peak power of over 100 gigawatts. We have demonstrated that our approach is a viable method for producing isolated attosecond pulses, and predict that further advancements using more advanced laser technology could lead to the development of a compact, high-energy attosecond source capable of producing pulses with durations of tens of attoseconds, a requirement for enabling the observation of electronic motion at the atomic level. We investigate how initial conditions with specific properties evolve over time in this setting. Specifically, we show that solutions to the equation will experience an exponential expansion in a particular time interval, and our analysis reveals a critical value for the equation's parameters that influences this expansion's extent. When the parameter exceeds this critical value, solutions will bypass the obstacle and concentrate energy in a particular region, leading to an infinite amount of energy within a bounded area of the solution space. We also identify a critical value for the equation's parameters that marks the onset of an exponential expansion in solutions, and under certain assumptions regarding the obstacle's shape, we demonstrate that an exponential expansion in solutions will occur consistently for all sufficiently small initial conditions. Physics-informed neural networks offer an innovative solution for partial differential equations that combines adaptability and efficient incorporation of observed data. Although previous studies have optimized the network architecture by adjusting its width and depth, the adaptation of its structure is still a relatively unexplored area of research. Our proposed method, Residual-based Adaptive creation of Nodes using Generalized activation functions, enables a more efficient use of resources by adding new parameters and nonlinear units based on a dynamic prediction error. This novel approach allows for continuous adjustments to be made in a dynamic environment. Our numerical evaluations, conducted on a variety of differential equations including some with singular solutions, reveal that this proposed framework is highly competitive. Additionally, we discovered that our proposed method identifies the minimal necessary number of components to accurately solve a given problem. This attribute, combined with its ability to regularly regularize the solution, makes it well-suited for solving forward and backward in time. Ultimately, our proposed method, known as RANG, represents a highly effective solution for solving a wide array of partial differential equations. This study examines the behavior and simulation of multi-domain ferroelectric FETs by investigating the impact of a key phenomenon: the shift in domain wall location due to electrostatic potential variation. We analyze how this shift influences the device's electrical properties and demonstrate that it's a crucial consideration for accurate device modeling. Furthermore, our research shows that the typical assumption of domain wall fixed position in conventional ferroelectric models is indeed inaccurate, especially at high capacitance voltages, where the effect becomes predominant. We confirm the validity of our findings through experimental evidence from oxiclad FeFETs. Additionally, our study highlights the significant adverse consequences that the dynamic movement of domain walls may have on the performance predictions of ferroelectric 2D materials, leading to inaccuracies in parameters such as I-V characteristics, flexibility, and scalability. Notably, although dynamic domain wall behavior may induce instability in ferroelectric memories, in ferroelectric FETs, this behavior can actually increase switching resistance, ultimately resulting in better performance and lower leakage. In summary, this study is the first to recognize the significance of domain wall dynamics in ferroelectric behavior and its far-reaching implications for ferroelectric technology. It is expected that this new understanding will pave the way for breakthroughs in ferroelectric device development. Finally, our research provides a comprehensive model that accounts for the effects of dynamic domain walls and domain wall fractures, enabling more precise simulation of ferroelectric systems. By incorporating this model, our predictions match the actual test results from oxiclad FeFETs, serving as a reliable theoretical foundation for future research and development in ferroelectric technology. Ultimately, this study is anticipated to propel the ferroelectric technology era forward, enabling more reliable and high-performance ferroelectric devices in the future. As a result, ferroelectric devices are now closer to reaching their full potential in cutting-edge technology applications such as ferroelectric RAM, ferroelectric photovoltaics, ferroelectric sensing, and more. A significant portion of Android app functionality stems from utilizing third-party libraries, specifically Cargo libraries, to fill gaps in the Android API. However, this extensive use of libraries also introduces security vulnerabilities to Android apps. To address this issue, we developed a system to build a dependency graph for Cargo libraries and uncover novel vulnerability linkages. Our method employs a weakness detection technique and a weakness diffusion model to identify previously unreported sequence variations of vulnerabilities. Specifically, it combines cargo audit tool-powered vulnerability detection with graph-based analysis to spread vulnerability propagation. To build the dependency graph, we conducted a comprehensive study involving manually classifying 13% of Cargo library classes and automatically processing the remaining classes. Our experiment yielded positive results, identifying new vulnerability transmissions among popular Cargo libraries and confirming the value of manual code review in bug discovery. Moreover, we validated the efficacy of our approach by tracking down 94% of newly introduced vulnerabilities in the latest version of Cargo libraries, showcasing the significant contribution of our method in contemporary vulnerability assessment. Our research outcomes are accessible via an online interface for easy exploration. To further contribute to the security ecosystem, we are making the source code and vulnerability data transfer model open-source to facilitate collaboration and innovation. Our study has several practical implications, with recommendations for developers to implement regular code audits, library maintainers to integrate automatic vulnerability detection, and platform providers to integrate holistic vulnerability assessment tools. By transferring our knowledge to the security community, we aim to promote a more cohesive approach to contemporary vulnerability assessment. Moreover, we are transferring our research outcomes, including the vulnerability weakness graph and weakness diffusion models, to the security ecosystem to facilitate cooperative research and foster innovative applications. Our transferable assets include the weakness graph and associated numerical values, as well as the code for replicating our experiments and developing new features. This transfer of knowledge is meant to foster a more cohesive approach to contemporary vulnerability assessment and promote cooperative research among the security community. To date, our research outcomes have received 86 unique citations from the security ecosystem. Our transferable assets have attracted contributions from three distinct entities, fostering innovative applications and a more cohesive approach to contemporary vulnerability assessment. Moreover, our research outcomes have attracted collaborations from universities and industry entities, leading to the replication and extension of our initial findings on Cargo libraries. Our research demonstrates the value of replicating our approach on other ecosystem modules, with considerable potential for new discoveries. To promote a more cohesive approach to contemporary vulnerability assessment, we are making our research outcomes, including the weakness graph and associated numerical values, open-source and transferring them to the security ecosystem.

For a one-dimensional stochastic complex Ginzburg-Landau equation driven by pure leap noise with parameters in certain intervals, we establish the likelihood of irreducibility based on different conditions related to the drift and diffusion coefficients. This analysis is supported by two key Lemmas which enable us to organize the proof in a clear structure. Furthermore, our findings are substantiated by two specific examples. Ultimately, these results are demonstrated to be applicable in two distinct numerical simulation scenarios. Interestingly, our model exhibits irreducible behavior in both cases, and we verify convergence in both scenarios. A thorough understanding of the formation and evolution of terrestrial exoplanets is necessary for making accurate predictions of how these planets develop and change over time.  A crucial aspect of this process is the chemical composition of these planets, which is best determined by analyzing the abundance of volatile elements in the host star.  We have created a new statistical method that utilizes radial velocity measurements to estimate the abundance of these elements.  Applying this method to a sample of 12 stars that host terrestrial exoplanets, we have detected volatile element depletion in the stars with higher mass, which suggests that more massive stars experience greater convective activity in their interiors, resulting in the incorporation of volatile elements in the stars' photospheres.  We have observed a correlation between a star's radius and its metallicity, which indicates that stars with higher radii experience less convective activity in their interiors, confirming our initial findings.  Based on our estimates of planetary mass and the metallicity of the host stars, we have considered several scenarios for the chemical composition of the M8 planet, which hosts a massive rocky world, and found that this planet likely has a highly differentiated interior with a rocky core and a mantle rich in silicate glasses and partially melted materials.  Similarly, our analysis of the CoRoT-7b and Kepler-10b planets reveals highly differentiated interiors with rocky cores and mantles composed of silicate glasses and partially melted materials.  However, our study of the super-Earthy Kepler-37b reveals a less differentiated interior with a larger core and mantle composed of silicate glasses and water, which is facilitated by the planet's high surface temperature and water-rich composition.  Our findings are consistent with the thesis that more massive terrestrial planets have volatile element-depleted interiors and exhibit less activity than smaller, less massive planets with richer volatile element compositions.  Finally, our analysis of various planetary mass ranges indicates that less massive planets are more likely to have water-rich compositions than their more massive counterparts, which is reflected in the preference for lower surface gravity in water-rich planets, as observed in the exoplanet inventory.  This research is an essential precursor to the utilization of transit photometry and asteroseismology in analyzing stellar and planetary internal structures and volatiles composition. Recent research has explored the effectiveness of attention mechanisms (AMs) within deep neural networks, revealing that AMs can accelerate model convergence and improve performance. This work investigates how the attention mechanism affects the convergence and performance of the channel state information (CSI)-based localization deep neural network. To this end, we present a new perspective on the attention mechanism's behavior, and provide evidence supporting this perspective through numerical analysis. Specifically, we demonstrate that the attention mechanism can be viewed as a heuristic function, driving the deep neural network to utilize input features that are highly relevant to the target output. By numerically evaluating this hypothesis, we reveal that attentioned channels are indeed closer to the network's predicted geolocation than non-attentioned channels. Consequently, the attention mechanism is effectively selecting the most influential signals for the geolocation prediction. Moreover, the attention mechanism also accelerates model convergence by optimizing signal propagation parameters. Our research provides new insights into the role of attention mechanisms within deep neural networks, and offers a fresh understanding of the benefits observed in previous research. These evaluation tools enable deeper analysis of attention mechanisms during the design and training process. Building on these insights, we propose a novel training strategy to develop channels (CSGs) that aid attention mechanism learning.
